dotPoints.description: Apply the key features of an object-oriented programming (OOP) language (objects; classes; encapsulation; abstraction; inheritance; generalisation; polymorphism)

prompts.question: Apply the key features of an OOP language to outline how a Vehicle class and a Car subclass could represent the fleet in this program.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A car-hire company is building a program to track its fleet. Each vehicle needs a mileage value that the program must protect from incorrect changes, and cars and electric cars share many of the same features.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Applies the key OOP features accurately to the fleet scenario, with a specific example of each feature used
3 marks: Applies three OOP features to the fleet scenario with relevant examples, though one link is underdeveloped
2 marks: Identifies two OOP features and links them to the fleet scenario with some detail
1 mark: Identifies one OOP feature with a basic link to the fleet scenario
markerNotes: Strong answers apply each feature to the car-hire fleet rather than defining it in general terms.
Award credit for showing how encapsulation protects mileage through a public method that validates the new value.
Reward accurate use of inheritance and generalisation, such as a Car subclass receiving the Vehicle features.
commonStudentErrors: Defining the OOP features in general terms without applying them to the fleet program.
Confusing a class, which is the blueprint, with an object, which is an instance created from it.
Describing inheritance as copying code by hand rather than a subclass receiving the superclass features.

sampleAnswers.answer: Classes such as Vehicle are blueprints that define the attributes and methods shared by all vehicles. Each vehicle in the fleet is an object created from this class, such as one car with its own registration and mileage. Encapsulation keeps mileage private, so it can only change through a public method that checks the new value. Abstraction hides this checking from the hire staff, who call only the public method. The Car subclass uses inheritance to receive the Vehicle features, an example of generalisation, and it overrides calculateHireCost() to show polymorphism. These OOP features make the fleet program reliable and easier to extend.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Applies all the key features accurately, with a specific fleet example for each one, which meets the full-mark standard. Keep each example tied to the fleet so the links stay precise.

sampleAnswers.answer: Each vehicle is an object created from a Vehicle class, which stores its registration and mileage. Encapsulation keeps the mileage private, so it can only be changed through a method.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies two OOP features and links them to the fleet, which meets the 2-mark standard. Add inheritance or polymorphism with a fleet example to reach the higher rows.

sampleAnswers.answer: Vehicles are stored as objects in the program.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies one OOP feature with a basic link to the fleet, which meets the 1-mark standard. Explain how a class or encapsulation protects the data to show a second feature.

prompts.question: Analyse how the OOP features of abstraction, inheritance, generalisation and polymorphism work together to make the library program easier to extend.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A regional library has an OOP program that manages loans of books. Staff want to add audiobooks and e-books later without rewriting the existing code.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses how abstraction, inheritance, generalisation and polymorphism interact in the library program, with precise links to the goal of extending it safely
5 marks: Analyses how several OOP features interact in the library program with relevant examples, though one link to extension is underdeveloped
4 marks: Explains two or three OOP features with examples linked to the library program, with limited analysis of how they work together
3 marks: Describes OOP features with relevant examples, but the links to the library program are general
2 marks: Identifies OOP features with a brief reference to the library program
1 mark: Makes a basic statement about OOP features without linking them to the library
markerNotes: Strong answers analyse how the features work together to support extension, rather than defining each feature separately.
Reward precise examples such as a LibraryItem superclass shared by Book and AudioBook classes.
Credit answers that note a limitation, such as subclasses still depending on the superclass design.
commonStudentErrors: Defining each feature in turn without explaining how they interact.
Claiming that inheritance means copying the superclass code into each subclass.
Describing polymorphism as a class having several names rather than one method acting differently for each object type.

sampleAnswers.answer: Abstraction lets the library program treat every loan item through one interface, such as a checkOut() method, so the desk code does not need to know how each item stores its data. Generalisation identifies the features all items share, such as a title and a due date, and places them in a LibraryItem superclass. Inheritance lets the Book, AudioBook and EBook classes reuse these features rather than repeat them, so a change to the superclass updates every subclass. Polymorphism lets the same call, such as getLoanPeriod(), return a different period for each object type, so an e-book can have a shorter loan than a book. Encapsulation keeps each item's loan status private, so only its own methods can change it, which reduces errors as new types are added. Together these OOP features mean new objects can be added with minimal change to existing code, the main long-term advantage for the library.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Analyses how the four features interact to support extension, with precise links to the library, which meets the full-mark standard. Name the single change each feature protects against to make the analysis sharper.

sampleAnswers.answer: Abstraction lets staff call one checkOut() method on any item without knowing how each type stores its data. Inheritance lets the Book and AudioBook classes reuse the title and due date from a LibraryItem superclass, which is generalisation of the shared features. Polymorphism means getLoanPeriod() returns a different period for each object type. Encapsulation keeps the loan status private to each item.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains four OOP features with relevant library examples, which meets the 4-mark standard. Add how the features work together to make the program easier to extend to reach the top rows.

sampleAnswers.answer: Inheritance means the AudioBook class gets the title from LibraryItem. Polymorphism means one method name can work for several classes.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies two OOP features with brief examples, which meets the 2-mark standard. Explain how these features support adding new item types to reach higher marks.

dotPoints.description: Compare procedural programming with OOP

prompts.question: Classify each version as procedural programming or OOP, and give one feature of each that supports your decision.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A junior developer has written two versions of a student grade program. Version 1 stores each student's name and marks in separate lists and uses functions that take those lists as arguments. Version 2 defines a Student class in which each object stores its own name and marks and calculates its own average.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Classifies both versions correctly and gives a specific feature of each that supports the decision
2 marks: Classifies both versions correctly, with a general reason for one or both decisions
1 mark: Classifies one version correctly with a basic reason
markerNotes: Strong answers classify each version on the evidence in its structure, such as whether data and operations are grouped together.
Reward a feature named precisely, such as the Student class bundling name, marks and average.
Credit answers that avoid calling Version 1 bad code, since the question asks about the paradigm rather than quality.
commonStudentErrors: Classifying Version 2 as procedural programming because it also uses functions.
Giving a general benefit of OOP, such as readability, rather than a feature shown in the code.
Confusing a class, which is the blueprint, with an object, which is one instance of it.

sampleAnswers.answer: Version 1 is procedural programming because its functions act on separate lists, so the data is not grouped with the operations on it. Version 2 is OOP because the Student class bundles each student's name and marks with the methods that calculate the average. Each object manages its own data, which is an example of encapsulation.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Classifies both versions correctly and gives a specific feature of each, which meets the full-mark standard. Keep naming the feature that drives the decision, such as the grouping in the class.

sampleAnswers.answer: Version 1 is procedural programming because it uses functions on separate lists. Version 2 is OOP because it uses a Student class.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Classifies both versions correctly with a general reason for each, which meets the 2-mark standard. Name what the Student class does, such as storing each student's marks, to reach full marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Version 2 is OOP because it uses a class.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Classifies one version correctly with a basic reason, but does not classify Version 1. Give a classification and a reason for both versions.

prompts.question: Compare how procedural programming and OOP would organise the stock data and its operations when new product types are added to the program.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A small business is deciding whether to rebuild its stock-control program. The current procedural program keeps stock data in shared global arrays, and its functions read and write those arrays directly. The owner plans to add new product types next year.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Compares both approaches in detail, showing how each organises data and operations and why this affects extending the stock program
5 marks: Compares both approaches with relevant detail, though the effect on extension is only partly developed
4 marks: Compares the two approaches with some relevant detail, with limited explanation of how they affect the program
3 marks: Describes a feature of each approach with a general link to the stock program
2 marks: Identifies a feature of each approach with limited comparison
1 mark: Makes a basic statement about one approach without comparison
markerNotes: Strong answers compare the two paradigms on the same criteria, such as data organisation, reuse and the effect of change.
Reward answers that link the comparison to adding product types in the stock program rather than to general advantages.
Accept that procedural programming can be simpler for a small program, provided the comparison stays balanced.
commonStudentErrors: Describing each paradigm separately without comparing them.
Stating that OOP is always better without linking this to the stock program.
Treating a class as the same thing as an object.
Claiming that procedural programming cannot use functions, which it relies on.

sampleAnswers.answer: Procedural programming would keep the stock data in shared arrays, with functions that read and write those arrays directly. Each new product type would need extra branches in many functions, so a change would spread across the whole program and increase the risk of errors. OOP would organise each product type as a class, bundling its stock data with the operations that use it, so each product is an object that manages its own stock level. Encapsulation would keep each object's stock level private and changed only through its own methods, so a new product type can be added as a subclass without altering existing code. Inheritance would let a Perishable class reuse the common features of a general Product class. Procedural programming is simpler for a small program, but OOP is better suited to adding product types because its changes are localised and easier to test. For this business, OOP gives the more maintainable structure.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Compares both approaches in detail and links each to adding product types, which meets the full-mark standard. Keep the comparison balanced by acknowledging where procedural programming is simpler.

sampleAnswers.answer: Procedural programming uses functions that work on shared arrays, so a new product type means changing several functions. OOP groups the stock data with its methods in a class, so each product is an object that manages its own stock level. Encapsulation makes this grouping safer, and new product types can be added as subclasses.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Compares the two approaches with relevant detail, but the effect on extending the program is only partly developed. Explain why changes stay localised in OOP to reach the top rows.

sampleAnswers.answer: Procedural programming uses functions and shared data, while OOP uses classes and objects.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies a feature of each approach with limited comparison, and does not link either to the stock program. Explain how the difference affects adding product types.

dotPoints.description: Use data flow diagrams, structure charts and class diagrams to represent a system

prompts.question: Describe what each of the three representations would show about the canteen system.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A school canteen wants a program for online lunch orders. Students choose items from a menu, the program checks stock before accepting each order, and the canteen manager receives a daily summary. The development team plans to use a data flow diagram, a structure chart and a class diagram to represent the system.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes what each of the three representations shows about the canteen system, with a specific element of the system for each
2 marks: Describes what two of the representations show about the canteen system, with a general reference to its parts
1 mark: Identifies one representation and a basic feature that it shows
markerNotes: Strong answers say what each representation shows about the canteen, such as orders flowing to the stock check or the Order class.
Reward reference to specific canteen elements, such as the menu, the stock check or the daily summary, rather than general features.
commonStudentErrors: Giving a definition of each diagram type without saying what it shows about the canteen system.
Describing a structure chart as a flowchart of steps rather than a hierarchy of modules.
Describing a data flow diagram as the order of program steps rather than how data moves between processes and stores.

sampleAnswers.answer: A data flow diagram shows the external entities, such as the student, the processes such as the stock check, the data stores, and the data flows between them. A structure chart shows the modules of the canteen system in a top-down hierarchy, with arrows for the data passed between modules. A class diagram shows classes such as Order and MenuItem, with their attributes, methods and relationships.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes what each representation shows, with a specific canteen element for each, which meets the full-mark standard. Keep each element named, as the examples here do.

sampleAnswers.answer: A data flow diagram shows how orders and stock data move between processes and stores. A class diagram shows the classes and their attributes in the system.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes two representations with a general reference to the system, which meets the 2-mark standard. Add the structure chart and a specific canteen element for each diagram to reach full marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: A structure chart shows the modules in the system.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies one representation and a basic feature it shows. Explain what the modules represent in the canteen system to build the answer.

prompts.question: Justify whether the team should prepare all three of a data flow diagram, a structure chart and a class diagram to represent the bus app before coding begins.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A small team is designing a mobile app that shows live bus timetables, stores users' saved routes, and will later gain a ticketing module. The team lead must decide which representations to prepare before programming starts, and the time for design work is limited.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Makes a well-reasoned judgement on whether all three representations are needed, with precise reasons linked to the bus app's data, modules and classes
5 marks: Makes a judgement on the choice of representations, supported by relevant reasons, though one reason is only partly developed
4 marks: Justifies the choice of representations with some relevant reasons, but the judgement is limited or not fully supported
3 marks: Describes what each representation shows with a general link to the bus app, without reaching a judgement
2 marks: Identifies a representation with a brief reason for its use
1 mark: Makes a basic statement about one representation without linking it to the app
markerNotes: Strong answers make a clear judgement about whether all three representations are needed, and support it with reasons.
Reward reasons that tie each representation to a specific part of the bus app, such as the timetable module or the ticketing module.
A justification must weigh the choice, such as the cost of rework, rather than only listing what each diagram shows.
commonStudentErrors: Listing what each diagram shows without making a judgement on the choice.
Stating that one diagram is always best without linking this to the bus app.
Confusing a structure chart, which shows modules and the data passed between them, with a class diagram.

sampleAnswers.answer: The team should prepare all three representations, because each one answers a different question about the bus app. A data flow diagram shows how timetable data and saved routes move between users, processes and data stores, so it confirms that no required data is missing from the design. A structure chart divides the app into modules, such as a timetable module and a ticketing module, and shows the data passed between them, which supports top-down planning. A class diagram shows the classes, such as Route and Stop, with their attributes, methods and relationships, which the team needs before the ticketing module is added safely. Using only one representation would leave gaps: a data flow diagram does not show the program structure, while a class diagram does not show how data moves through the system. The extra design time is small compared with the cost of rework later, so the decision is justified.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Makes a well-reasoned judgement with precise reasons linked to the modules, data and classes, which meets the full-mark standard. Keep weighing the cost of each choice against the benefit, as the final sentence does.

sampleAnswers.answer: The team should prepare all three, because a data flow diagram shows how data moves and a structure chart shows the modules. A class diagram is also useful for the ticketing module. Using only one would leave gaps in the design of the system, although the extra time is a real cost.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Justifies the choice with some relevant reasons, but the judgement is not fully supported. Explain what would be missed for each single diagram to reach the top rows.

sampleAnswers.answer: The team should use a class diagram because it shows the classes. A data flow diagram shows the data.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies a representation with a brief reason for its use. Give a reason that ties the diagram to the bus app to build the answer.

dotPoints.description: Describe the process of design used to develop code in an OOP language (task definition; top-down and bottom-up; facade pattern; agility)

prompts.question: Outline the first stages of the design process the team should follow, and where a facade pattern and agility fit within it.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A sports club is building an OOP program to manage memberships and court bookings. The project lead wants the team to plan the program's structure before writing code, and the club's needs may change during the year.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Outlines the design stages from task definition through top-down and bottom-up design to the facade pattern and agility, with a brief point for each
2 marks: Outlines two stages of the design process, with a brief description of each
1 mark: Identifies one stage of the design process with a basic description
markerNotes: Strong answers present the design process as an ordered sequence, starting with task definition.
Reward accurate, brief descriptions of the facade pattern as one simplified interface to a complex subsystem.
Accept agility described as short, iterative cycles that respond to feedback.
commonStudentErrors: Listing the terms without saying what each involves.
Describing the facade pattern as a visual layout or user interface design.
Treating top-down and bottom-up design as the same approach.

sampleAnswers.answer: In this design process, task definition comes first, stating the program's inputs, outputs and processing before design begins. Top-down design then breaks the OOP program into major tasks, while bottom-up design builds and tests small classes that are combined. A facade pattern gives other parts of the program one simple class to call, hiding a complex subsystem, and agility means working in short iterations that respond to feedback.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Outlines the stages in a logical sequence with a brief point for each, which meets the full-mark standard. Keep each point short and accurate, as the facade and agility descriptions are here.

sampleAnswers.answer: Task definition sets the program's inputs and outputs first. Top-down design then breaks the program into smaller tasks.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Outlines two stages of the design process with brief descriptions, which meets the 2-mark standard. Add where the facade pattern and agility fit to reach full marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Top-down design breaks the program into smaller parts.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies one stage of the design process with a basic description. Add a second stage, such as task definition, to build the outline.

prompts.question: Discuss how task definition, top-down and bottom-up design, the facade pattern and agility can be combined in the design process for this program.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A club's programming team has a fixed deadline for a membership and booking program. Some members prefer to design the whole structure first, while others want to build small parts and test them early.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Discusses how the design approaches combine in an OOP design process, with relevant reasons for each element and a reasoned conclusion
4 marks: Discusses several elements of the design process with relevant reasons, though the links between the approaches are underdeveloped
3 marks: Explains some elements of the design process with a general link to the OOP program
2 marks: Describes a design approach with a brief description and limited reference to the program
1 mark: Makes a basic statement about the design process without detail
markerNotes: Strong answers discuss the trade-offs between top-down and bottom-up design rather than describing each in isolation.
Reward links between agility and the iterative revision of the design.
Look for a reasoned conclusion about the combined approach, not a summary of the terms.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the terms without discussing how they combine in an OOP design process.
Stating that agile development means no design is needed.
Claiming the facade pattern is a type of graphical design.

sampleAnswers.answer: Task definition should come first, because it fixes the inputs, outputs and processing the design must meet. Top-down design then breaks the OOP program into major components, such as booking and membership, and refines each until the classes can be written. Bottom-up design works in the opposite direction, building and testing small classes first so they can be combined. Together, the two approaches let the team plan the overall structure while proving the detail early. A facade pattern supports this by giving other parts of the program one simple class that hides a complex subsystem, so bottom-up parts can change safely. Agility suits the approach because short iterations allow the design to be revised as feedback arrives, although too little upfront planning can weaken it. Overall, a combined top-down and bottom-up design process within an agile approach gives the best balance of planning and adaptation.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Discusses how the elements combine and reaches a reasoned conclusion, which meets the full-mark standard. Keep the trade-off visible, as the closing sentence does.

sampleAnswers.answer: Task definition sets the inputs and outputs first. Top-down design breaks the program into parts, while bottom-up design builds small classes first. A facade pattern hides complexity behind one class, and agility allows the design to change through short cycles.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains some elements of the design process with a general link to the program, which meets the 3-mark standard. Discuss how the approaches combine and reach a conclusion to reach the top rows.

sampleAnswers.answer: Top-down design breaks the program into parts.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Makes a basic statement about one element without discussion. Add how it combines with another element to build the answer.

dotPoints.description: Assess the effectiveness of programming code developed to implement an algorithm

prompts.question: Describe three measures the student could use to check the effectiveness of this programming code, and link each measure to the method.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student has written an OOP method that finds the largest mark in a list of exam marks. The algorithm sets the largest value to the first mark, compares each remaining mark with it, and replaces it when a larger mark is found. The method returns correct results for most lists but fails when the list is empty.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes three measures of effectiveness, each linked to a specific feature of the method, such as the empty list or the comparisons
2 marks: Describes two measures of effectiveness with a general link to the method
1 mark: Identifies one measure of effectiveness with a basic link to the method
markerNotes: Strong answers name a measure, such as correctness, robustness or efficiency, and link it to the student's method.
Reward reference to the empty-list failure as evidence that robustness testing is needed.
commonStudentErrors: Describing testing in general terms without saying what to test in this method.
Describing efficiency as whether the code is correct rather than how many resources it uses.
Stating that the code is effective because it has comments or a clear name.

sampleAnswers.answer: Correctness can be checked by testing the method with known lists, such as lists with negative or repeated marks, to confirm it returns the largest mark. Robustness can be checked by testing the empty list that currently fails, so the method handles it safely. Efficiency can be measured by counting comparisons, which should grow with the list length for this algorithm. Together, these measures show the effectiveness of the programming code.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes three measures, each linked to a feature of the method, which meets the full-mark standard. Keep each test tied to a specific input, as the empty list and repeated marks are here.

sampleAnswers.answer: Correctness can be checked by testing known lists, such as lists with repeated marks. Robustness can be checked by testing the empty list, which currently fails.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes two measures with a link to the method, which meets the 2-mark standard. Add a third measure, such as efficiency, to reach full marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Correctness can be checked by testing the method.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies one measure with a basic link to the method. Describe how the test would be run, using a list from the scenario.

prompts.question: Assess the effectiveness of this programming code as an implementation of its sorting algorithm.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A development team has written an OOP program that sorts a list of 10,000 customer orders using nested loops, which compare every pair of orders. The code passes all unit tests and returns the orders in the correct sequence, but it takes several minutes to finish and contains several duplicated blocks of code.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Assesses the effectiveness of the code against correctness, efficiency and maintainability, with a reasoned overall judgement supported by specific evidence from the scenario
5 marks: Assesses the effectiveness of the code with relevant evidence for at least two criteria, though the overall judgement is only partly supported
4 marks: Discusses some strengths and weaknesses of the code with relevant evidence, but the assessment is not fully reasoned
3 marks: Describes one or two features of the code with a general comment on effectiveness
2 marks: Identifies one strength or weakness of the code with limited explanation
1 mark: Makes a basic statement about the code without supporting evidence
markerNotes: Strong answers judge the code against named criteria such as correctness, efficiency and maintainability, rather than giving a general opinion.
Reward evidence drawn from the scenario, such as the nested loops and the duplicated blocks.
A reasoned overall judgement is needed, showing which weaknesses matter most for a live ordering system.
commonStudentErrors: Declaring the code good or bad without criteria or evidence.
Assessing only correctness and ignoring efficiency and maintainability.
Stating that a correct program is always effective, regardless of its speed.

sampleAnswers.answer: The code is effective in correctness, because it passes all unit tests and returns the orders in the correct sequence, so the sorting algorithm is implemented faithfully. Its efficiency is weak, however. The nested loops compare every pair of orders, so the number of comparisons grows with the square of the number of orders, and with 10,000 orders the program takes several minutes. The duplicated blocks make the programming code harder to maintain, since a change to one copy may be missed. Unless the tests include unusual inputs, robustness has not been shown. To improve the effectiveness of the code, the team should replace the nested loops with a more efficient sorting algorithm, merge the duplicated blocks into one method, and add edge-case tests. On balance, the code is effective in correctness but not yet effective overall.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Assesses the code against correctness, efficiency and maintainability with a reasoned overall judgement, which meets the full-mark standard. Keep the judgement tied to evidence, as the closing sentence does.

sampleAnswers.answer: The code implements the sorting algorithm correctly, as shown by the passing unit tests. However, the nested loops compare every pair of orders, so the program is slow with 10,000 orders and its efficiency is weak. The duplicated blocks also make the programming code harder to maintain, so the effectiveness of the code is limited.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Discusses strengths and weaknesses with relevant evidence, but the assessment is not fully reasoned. Weigh the weaknesses against each other and reach an overall judgement to reach the top rows.

sampleAnswers.answer: The code is correct because it passes the tests, but it is slow with many orders.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies one strength and one weakness with limited explanation, which meets the 2-mark standard. Add the cause of the slowness and a judgement to build the answer.

dotPoints.description: Investigate how OOP languages handle message-passing between objects

prompts.question: Describe how one object sends a message to another in an OOP language, using the Order and Payment objects in this program.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: An OOP program for a school canteen has an Order object and a Payment object. When a student confirms an order, the Order object must ask the Payment object to process the total amount.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes how the Order object sends a message by calling a public method, including the parameter passed and the response from the Payment object
2 marks: Describes how one object calls a method of another object, with limited detail about the response
1 mark: Identifies that objects communicate by calling methods
markerNotes: Strong answers describe the sequence: the sending object calls a public method, passes parameters and receives a response.
Reward accurate use of message and method, showing that a message is a request to another object.
commonStudentErrors: Describing one object directly changing another object's private data rather than calling a public method.
Confusing message-passing between objects with messages sent between computers on a network.

sampleAnswers.answer: The Order object sends a message to the Payment object by calling one of its public methods, such as processPayment(total), and passing the amount as a parameter. The Payment object runs its own code in response and returns a result, such as success or failure. This message-passing works in an OOP language because the Payment object's data stays encapsulated, so the Order object never changes it directly.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes the message, the parameter and the response, which meets the full-mark standard. Keep the description to the sequence of call, parameter and response, as here.

sampleAnswers.answer: The Order object calls a public method of the Payment object and passes the total. The Payment object then returns a result.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes how one object calls a method of another, with limited detail about the response, which meets the 2-mark standard. Name the parameter and explain the result to reach 3 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: The Order object calls a method on the Payment object.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies that objects communicate by calling methods. Add the parameter and the response to build the description.

prompts.question: Analyse how message-passing between objects allows the team to change the Scoreboard object without breaking the Player and Sound classes.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A team of four programmers is building an OOP game in which a Player object, a Scoreboard object and a Sound object must communicate. The team needs to change how the Scoreboard object updates its score without affecting the other classes.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Analyses how message-passing lets the team change the Scoreboard object through public methods, with precise links to the Player and Sound classes and to the limits of the approach
4 marks: Analyses how message-passing supports the change with relevant examples, though one link or the limits of the approach are underdeveloped
3 marks: Explains how objects send messages and receive responses, with some examples but limited analysis of the team's change
2 marks: Describes message-passing with a general link to the game, without analysing the team's change
1 mark: Makes a basic statement about objects without referring to messages
markerNotes: Strong answers analyse the effect of message-passing on the team's change, rather than defining the term.
Reward reasons drawn from the scenario, such as the Player object relying only on the public method names.

sampleAnswers.answer: In an OOP language, objects communicate through message-passing: one object invokes a public method of another, passing any parameters needed, and the receiving object returns a result. This helps the team because the Player object does not need to know how the Scoreboard object stores its score; it sends a message such as addPoints(10) and receives the updated total. Encapsulation keeps the score data private, so the Scoreboard internals can be rewritten while its public methods stay the same. The other classes keep sending the same messages and receiving the same kinds of responses, so they need no change. However, message-passing has limits: if a method name or parameter changes, every calling object must be updated, and long chains of messages can make the program harder to trace. The team should therefore fix the method signatures before programming begins.

dotPoints.description: Design and implement computer programs involving branching, iteration and functions in an OOP language for an identified need or opportunity

prompts.question: Construct the pseudocode for a function in an Order class that returns the total price of an order, using iteration over the items and branching for the discount.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A cafe owner needs a program to calculate the total price of a customer order. Each item has a price and a quantity, and a 10 per cent discount applies to an item only when its quantity is 3 or more.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Constructs a correct, complete function that uses iteration to total the items and branching to apply the discount accurately, with a return value
3 marks: Constructs a function that uses iteration and branching, with one error or omission in the discount or the total
2 marks: Constructs a function that uses iteration to total the items, without the discount
1 mark: Identifies a function header or a basic loop structure for the total
markerNotes: Strong answers use a loop to visit every item and an IF statement with the correct quantity condition.
Reward correct pseudocode structure, such as a return value and clear variable names.
commonStudentErrors: Applying the discount to every item regardless of quantity.
Omitting the return statement so the total is never passed back.
Using a condition of greater than 3 when the scenario says 3 or more.

sampleAnswers.answer:
This OOP language design places the discount rule in the Order class. The pseudocode is:
FUNCTION TotalPrice()
  total <- 0
  FOR EACH item IN items
    cost <- item.price * item.quantity
    IF item.quantity >= 3 THEN
      cost <- cost * 0.9
    END IF
    total <- total + cost
  END FOR
  RETURN total
END FUNCTION
The iteration visits every item, and the branching applies the discount only when the quantity is 3 or more. The function returns the total so the computer program can display it, which implements the requirement.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Constructs a complete function with iteration, branching and a return value, which meets the full-mark standard. Keep the condition as 3 or more, as written, so the discount is applied correctly.

  total <- 0
  FOR EACH item IN items
    total <- total + item.price * item.quantity
  END FOR
  RETURN total
END FUNCTION
This loops through each item to total the price.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Constructs a function that totals the items with iteration, which meets the 2-mark standard. Add an IF statement that applies the 10 per cent discount when the quantity is 3 or more to reach full marks.

Keeping the branch in the main program would repeat the logic in several places, making the change harder to implement correctly. A very small program might not need a separate function, but for a program the cafe will maintain for years, the separation is justified because it improves testing, reuse and maintenance.

sampleAnswers.answer: The mix of black box testing and white box testing is effective in part. In manufacturing, robotic arms with servo motors and encoders position parts on an assembly line. In healthcare, surgical robots use sensors and actuators to guide instruments with fine control. In agriculture, automated milking systems use sensors to locate each teat and actuators to attach the cups.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Outlines three distinct specialised fields, each with a named mechatronic system and a brief description of its function, which meets the full-mark standard. The answer could name the system more precisely, such as a specific type of surgical robot.

sampleAnswers.answer: Two specialised fields are manufacturing and healthcare. In manufacturing, a robotic arm assembles parts on a production line. In healthcare, a surgical robot helps doctors perform precise operations.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Outlines two correct specialised fields, each with a named system, but the answer does not add a third field and the descriptions are brief. Expand the descriptions to show how sensors or actuators enable the system to work.

sampleAnswers.answer: Healthcare, where surgical robots are used in operating theatres.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies one specialised field with a relevant system, which earns one mark. Add two more fields, each with its own example system, to outline the full answer.

prompts.question: Discuss how mechatronic systems benefit workers and the wider community in one specialised field, and include at least one limitation of their use.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A regional hospital is considering a mechatronic system with sensors, motorised actuators and a control program to help nurses move patients safely. The hospital board wants a balanced view of the benefits and limitations before it makes a decision.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Discusses benefits for workers and the community in one specialised field, and a limitation of use, with sustained and well-linked reasoning supported by a specific example
4 marks: Discusses at least one benefit and one limitation in one specialised field, with a relevant example and clear reasoning for most points
3 marks: Discusses a benefit and a limitation of the systems, with a brief example or limited development of the reasoning
2 marks: Describes one benefit or one limitation of mechatronic systems with little development
1 mark: Makes a basic statement that mechatronic systems are useful, without a field or a reason
markerNotes: Benefits should be linked to workers and to the wider community, such as safer patient handling or more consistent care.
A strong answer weighs at least one limitation, such as cost, training needs or the risk of faults, and does not simply list advantages.
Reward examples drawn from the scenario and a named specialised field rather than general claims about technology.
commonStudentErrors: Listing benefits without discussing them or linking them to workers or the community.
Describing a limitation without showing how it affects the field or the users.
Making general claims about robots rather than a mechatronic system in one specialised field.
Treating the answer as one-sided by ignoring limitations entirely.

sampleAnswers.answer: In the specialised field of healthcare, applications of mechatronic systems can benefit nurses and the wider community. A patient-handling system uses sensors to detect the patient's position and actuators to lift the patient under a control program. This reduces manual lifting for nurses, which lowers the risk of injury, and allows patients to be moved more consistently, supporting safer care. Patients and their families also benefit from gentler and more consistent handling. However, there are limitations. The purchase and maintenance costs are high, which may restrict access for smaller hospitals, and staff need training to operate the system safely. A software fault or sensor failure could also cause unsafe movement, so backup procedures and regular safety checks are essential.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Discusses benefits for nurses and the community and a limitation in one specialised field, with a specific example and linked reasoning, which meets the full-mark standard. A tighter answer would explain why the training need matters to patient safety.

sampleAnswers.answer: Mechatronic systems can reduce manual lifting for nurses, which benefits workers. However, they are costly to buy and maintain, which limits their use in smaller hospitals.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Discusses a benefit and a limitation with a brief example, but the reasoning is limited and the answer does not link the benefit to the wider community. Developing the link to patients and the hospital would lift it.

sampleAnswers.answer: Mechatronic systems are useful in hospitals because they are modern.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Makes a basic statement without naming a benefit, a limitation or a reason. Name one specific benefit to workers and one limitation, each explained.

dotPoints.description: Identify the hardware requirements to run a program and the effect on code development (assessing the relationship of microcontrollers and the central processing unit (CPU); the influence of instruction set and opcodes; the use of address and data registers)

prompts.question: Describe how the central processing unit (CPU) of a microcontroller runs a program, including the hardware requirements a developer must consider.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A small engineering firm is writing control software for a battery-powered environmental sensor. The developer has been given a microcontroller board with limited memory and asks how the board's hardware will shape the code she writes.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Describes how the CPU and the other parts of the microcontroller run the program with accurate detail, and explains how the instruction set, opcodes or registers affect the code a developer writes
3 marks: Describes the relationship between the microcontroller and the CPU accurately, with one link to the instruction set, opcodes or registers
2 marks: Describes the microcontroller or the CPU with some accuracy, without explaining how the hardware affects code development
1 mark: Identifies one hardware component of a microcontroller without describing its relationship to the program
markerNotes: Strong answers describe the CPU as the part that fetches, decodes and executes instructions, and the microcontroller as a single chip that also holds memory and input/output circuits.
Link the hardware to code development, for example through limited registers, memory or the instruction set that the code must suit.
Use the terms accurately: opcodes are the operation codes within an instruction, while the instruction set is the full set of instructions a CPU can run.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the microcontroller and the CPU as the same thing, without noting that the microcontroller also holds memory and input/output circuits.
Mentioning registers without saying what they store or how they limit the code.
Describing hardware requirements, such as a faster clock, without linking them to code development.
Confusing opcodes with the instruction set, or with the data an instruction uses.

sampleAnswers.answer: A microcontroller integrates a CPU, memory and input/output circuits on one chip, and the central processing unit does the work of running the program. The CPU fetches each instruction from memory, decodes it and executes it, so every line of code must be translated into operations the CPU can carry out. The instruction set defines the opcodes the CPU recognises, so a developer must write or compile code that uses only those instructions. Address registers hold the memory locations to be read or written, while data registers hold the values being processed. Because these hardware requirements are tight on a small board, the developer must write efficient code and avoid unnecessary variables.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes the link between the microcontroller and the CPU in accurate detail and explains how the instruction set, opcodes and registers shape the code, which meets the full-mark standard. Naming the CPU's fetch-decode-execute cycle more directly would sharpen the answer.

sampleAnswers.answer: A microcontroller contains a CPU, memory and input/output circuits on one chip. The CPU runs the instructions of the program, one after another.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes the microcontroller and the CPU with some accuracy, but does not explain how the hardware affects code development, so it earns two marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: A microcontroller has a CPU.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Names one hardware component, which earns one mark. Explain what the CPU does with the program and how it works with memory and the instruction set.

prompts.question: Analyse how the instruction set and opcodes of a microcontroller's CPU affect the hardware requirements and the code a developer must write when the program moves to a different board.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A developer has written a motion-control program for a microcontroller and must now run the same program on a different board with a different CPU. The new board's CPU uses a different instruction set and has less memory available for code.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Analyses how differences in the instruction set and opcodes change the hardware requirements and the code a developer must write, supported by an accurate and specific example from the scenario
4 marks: Analyses the effect of the instruction set or opcodes on the code, with an accurate explanation of at least one resulting hardware requirement
3 marks: Explains that the instruction set affects the code a developer writes, with a brief link to the hardware requirements
2 marks: Describes the instruction set or opcodes with limited accuracy and no clear link to code development
1 mark: Identifies the instruction set as a feature of a CPU without explaining its effect
markerNotes: Reward answers that go beyond stating that the instruction set differs and explain what changes in the code, such as recompilation or more instructions per task.
The hardware link should be specific, for example memory limits or processing speed, not general claims that hardware matters.
Machine code is specific to an instruction set, so the source code may need recompiling rather than simply copying across.
commonStudentErrors: Saying the code will not work without explaining that machine code depends on the instruction set.
Confusing opcodes with the operands or data that an instruction uses.
Assuming a higher-level program runs unchanged on any CPU without recompilation.
Describing hardware differences without linking them to the code the developer must write.

sampleAnswers.answer: The new CPU has a different instruction set, so the opcodes recognised by the original central processing unit are no longer valid. Machine code compiled for the first microcontroller will not run on the new CPU, so the developer must recompile the source code with a compiler that targets the new instruction set. The hardware requirements also change. If the new instruction set needs more instructions to perform a routine that used a single opcode before, the code grows in size and may exceed the limited memory of the new board. The developer may therefore need to rewrite time-critical sections in a more efficient form and test each change on the motion hardware. This shows how the hardware requirements drive code development, since the instruction set shapes both what the program can run on and how much of the CPU's capacity it must use.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Analyses how the differing instruction set changes the opcodes, the hardware requirements and the code, with a specific example from the scenario, which meets the full-mark standard. Stating the memory consequence more precisely would strengthen the link further.

sampleAnswers.answer: A different instruction set means the opcodes change, so the old machine code will not run and the program must be recompiled, which may need more memory.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains that the instruction set affects the code and gives a brief link to memory, which earns three marks. It does not analyse the effect on the developer's rewrite of time-critical sections.

sampleAnswers.answer: The instruction set is a feature of the CPU.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies the instruction set without explaining its effect on the code, which earns one mark. Explain what the developer must change and why.

dotPoints.description: Identify and describe a range of sensors, actuators and end effectors/manipulators within existing mechatronic systems (motion sensors; light level sensors; hydraulic actuators; robotic grippers)

prompts.question: Classify each of the four components in the scenario as a sensor, an actuator or an end effector, giving its role in the station.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A small food packaging plant has an automated station with four components. A motion sensor detects when a tray arrives, a light level sensor switches on the inspection lamp when the area is dark, a hydraulic actuator pushes a stop into position, and a robotic gripper picks each product and places it in the tray.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Correctly classifies all four components, each with a brief statement of its role in the station
3 marks: Correctly classifies three of the four components, each with a brief statement of its role
2 marks: Correctly classifies two of the four components, with a brief statement of role for each
1 mark: Correctly classifies one component as a sensor, actuator or end effector
markerNotes: Classify each component by its function: a sensor detects an input, an actuator produces motion from an energy source, and an end effector is the tool at the end of a manipulator.
A strong answer ties each classification to the station, so the role in the scenario is clear.
The hydraulic actuator uses pressurised fluid, which distinguishes it from electric or pneumatic actuators.
commonStudentErrors: Classifying a light level sensor as an actuator because it switches the lamp.
Calling the robotic gripper an actuator rather than an end effector.
Giving a correct classification without a role in the station.
Describing a motion sensor as producing movement rather than detecting it.

sampleAnswers.answer: The motion sensor is a sensor because it detects the arrival of a tray and sends a signal to the controller. The light level sensor is also a sensor, because it measures ambient light and triggers the inspection lamp when the area is dark. The hydraulic actuator is an actuator, since it converts pressurised fluid into linear motion to push the stop into position. The robotic gripper is an end effector, because it sits at the end of the arm and grasps each product to place it in the tray.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Correctly classifies all four components with a clear role for each in the station, which meets the full-mark standard. Naming the robotic gripper's position on the manipulator would make the end effector classification even clearer.

sampleAnswers.answer: The motion sensor is a sensor because it detects the tray. The hydraulic actuator is an actuator because it moves the stop into position. The robotic gripper is an actuator because it moves the product.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Correctly classifies the motion sensor and the hydraulic actuator, each with a role, which earns two marks. The robotic gripper is an end effector, not an actuator, and the light level sensor is missing.

sampleAnswers.answer: The light level sensor is a sensor.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Correctly classifies one component, which earns one mark. Classify the other three components and give each one's role in the station.

prompts.question: Compare the operation of a motion sensor with that of a light level sensor in the same automated installation, showing how each provides input to the control system.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A school's automated courtyard light uses a motion sensor and a light level sensor to decide when to switch on a lamp. The facilities team wants to understand how each sensor contributes to that decision before it changes the system's settings.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Compares the motion sensor and the light level sensor with accurate detail, showing clear similarities and differences in what each measures and how it feeds the control system
4 marks: Compares both sensors accurately, with at least one clear difference and an explanation of how the control system uses each input
3 marks: Describes both sensors with some attempt to compare them, but the comparison is brief or only partly developed
2 marks: Describes one or both sensors with limited accuracy and no clear comparison
1 mark: Makes a basic statement about one sensor, such as that it detects movement, without comparison
markerNotes: A strong comparison addresses both similarities and differences, such as both producing an input signal but measuring different things.
Describe the operating principle of each sensor, such as infrared heat changes for a passive infrared motion sensor and resistance changes for a light-dependent resistor.
Explain how the control system combines the two inputs to make the lamp decision, rather than describing each sensor separately.
commonStudentErrors: Describing each sensor separately without any comparison.
Stating that a light level sensor detects movement, or that a motion sensor measures brightness.
Listing differences without showing how the control system uses each input.
Confusing the output of a sensor with the action of the lamp.

sampleAnswers.answer: A motion sensor and a light level sensor both provide input to the control system, but they measure different things. Both send a signal that the controller can act on, so neither operates the lamp directly. The motion sensor, often a passive infrared (PIR) device, detects changes in infrared heat from a moving person and produces a digital signal when movement occurs. The light level sensor, typically a light-dependent resistor, changes its resistance with the brightness of the courtyard, so the controller reads a varying voltage. The key difference is that the motion sensor responds to an event, whereas the light level sensor measures a continuous condition. The control system combines the two inputs: the lamp switches on only when the light level falls below a set threshold and the motion sensor detects movement.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Compares the two sensors with accurate detail, showing a clear similarity and difference in what each measures and how the control system combines them, which meets the full-mark standard. A brief note on the voltage divider would add technical precision.

sampleAnswers.answer: Both sensors send input to the controller. A motion sensor detects movement, while a light level sensor measures how bright the courtyard is, so the lamp only comes on in the dark.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes both sensors with a brief comparison, which earns three marks. The comparison is not developed, and the answer does not explain how the control system combines the two inputs.

sampleAnswers.answer: A motion sensor detects movement.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Makes a basic statement about one sensor, which earns one mark. A comparison needs both sensors, the difference between them, and how the control system uses each input.

dotPoints.description: Use different types of data and understand how it is obtained and processed in a mechatronic system, including diagnostic data and data used for optimisation

prompts.question: Calculate the mean motor current for the five cycles in the scenario, identify the cycle that is more than 0.5 A above that mean, and state what this diagnostic data may indicate about the motor.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A robotic welding cell records the current drawn by its positioning motor at the end of each of five production cycles as diagnostic data. The readings in amps are: cycle 1 = 4.2, cycle 2 = 4.4, cycle 3 = 4.3, cycle 4 = 4.6 and cycle 5 = 5.1.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Calculates the mean motor current as 4.52 A, identifies cycle 5 as the reading more than 0.5 A above the mean, and explains what this diagnostic data may indicate about the motor
2 marks: Calculates the mean correctly and identifies cycle 5, without a clear explanation of what the diagnostic data may indicate
1 mark: Calculates the mean motor current correctly, or identifies the cycle that exceeds the mean by more than 0.5 A without calculating the mean
markerNotes: Show the calculation (the sum divided by five) so that the mean can be checked, and give the answer as 4.52 A.
Interpretation should refer to the purpose of diagnostic data: an unexpected rise in motor current can signal friction, an obstruction or wear, which helps schedule maintenance.
Rewarded answers identify the cycle by its number and its reading, not just a value.
commonStudentErrors: Dividing by four rather than five cycles, or rounding the mean too early.
Identifying cycle 4 because it is the second highest value, without checking the 0.5 A threshold.
Stating that the motor is faulty, without linking the reading to possible causes.
Confusing diagnostic data with optimisation data, which is used to improve performance rather than to detect faults.

sampleAnswers.answer: The mean motor current is 4.52 A, from 22.6 A divided by five. Cycle 5 is the only reading more than 0.5 A above the mean, at 5.1 A, which is 0.58 A higher. As diagnostic data, this rise suggests increased friction, an obstruction or early wear in the mechatronic system, so the cell should be inspected before a fault stops production.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Calculates the mean correctly, identifies cycle 5 against the 0.5 A threshold, and explains what the diagnostic data may indicate, which meets the full-mark standard. Showing the sum of the five readings would make the calculation easier to check.

sampleAnswers.answer: The mean is 4.52 A, and cycle 5 at 5.1 A is the highest reading, so it stands out from the others.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Calculates the mean correctly and identifies cycle 5, which earns two marks. The answer does not state the 0.5 A threshold or explain what the reading may indicate about the motor.

sampleAnswers.answer: The mean is 4.52 A, found by adding the five readings and dividing by five.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Calculates the mean correctly, which earns one mark. The answer does not identify cycle 5 or interpret the diagnostic data.

prompts.question: Explain how diagnostic data and data used for optimisation differ in purpose, and how a technician could use each type to improve the performance of the mechatronic system.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A bottling line has a controller that records motor temperature, fault codes and cycle times for each run. The maintenance team wants to know which of these records should be used to find faults and which should be used to make the line run faster.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Explains the purpose of diagnostic and optimisation data, how each is obtained and processed, and how a technician would use each to improve the system, with precise and well-linked reasoning
4 marks: Explains the purpose of both types of data and how at least one is obtained or processed, with a relevant example of use
3 marks: Explains the purpose of one or both types of data with some reasoning, but how they are obtained or processed is only briefly addressed
2 marks: Describes one type of data with limited accuracy and little reason for its use
1 mark: Names one type of data without describing its purpose or how it is obtained
markerNotes: Diagnostic data is used to detect faults or predict failure, while optimisation data is used to improve speed, efficiency or quality. A strong answer keeps these purposes distinct.
Show how the data is obtained, for example from sensors and controller logs, and how it is processed, for example by comparing it with limits or averaging across cycles.
Link each type to a specific technician action, such as scheduling an inspection or adjusting a conveyor speed.
commonStudentErrors: Treating diagnostic and optimisation data as the same thing.
Explaining the purpose of the data without saying how it is obtained or processed.
Describing the data types only, without a technician action.
Stating that the data is collected by a computer without naming a sensor or controller.

sampleAnswers.answer: Diagnostic data and optimisation data differ in purpose. Diagnostic data, such as motor temperature and fault codes, is used to identify a component that is failing or likely to fail, so maintenance can be planned before a breakdown. Optimisation data, such as cycle times, is used to find ways to improve the performance of the mechatronic system without changing its basic function. Both types are obtained by sensors and the controller, which record measurements and events as they occur. They are processed differently: diagnostic data is compared with normal limits to trigger alerts, while optimisation data is averaged over many cycles and compared across settings. A technician could use the fault codes to schedule a motor inspection, and use the cycle times to adjust the speed of the conveyor.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains the purpose of both data types, how each is obtained and processed, and a specific technician action for each, which meets the full-mark standard. A closing sentence on the trade-off between the two uses would strengthen the answer.

sampleAnswers.answer: Diagnostic data, such as fault codes, shows whether a part is failing, while optimisation data, such as cycle times, helps the line run better. A technician could use the fault codes to plan repairs.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains the purpose of both types with some reasoning, which earns three marks. It does not explain how either type is obtained or processed, which the full-mark answer covers.

sampleAnswers.answer: Diagnostic data is one type recorded by the line.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Names one type of data without describing its purpose or how it is obtained, which earns one mark. Explain what the data shows and how it is recorded.

dotPoints.description: Experiment with software to control interactions and dependencies within mechatronic systems (motion constraints; degrees of freedom; combination of subsystems; combination of sensors, actuators and end effectors to create viable subsystems)

prompts.question: Apply the concept of degrees of freedom to the robotic arm in the scenario, stating how many degrees of freedom it has and how the shoulder stop limits its motion.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A school robotics team has built a three-joint arm for a competition. The base rotates about a vertical axis, the shoulder and elbow each rotate within the same vertical plane, and a mechanical stop prevents the shoulder from rotating more than 90 degrees. The arm has no separate gripper.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Applies the concept of degrees of freedom to count three independent movements correctly and explains how the shoulder stop limits movement to a defined range, using accurate terminology
3 marks: Counts three degrees of freedom correctly and describes the effect of the shoulder stop on movement
2 marks: States the correct number of degrees of freedom without explaining the shoulder stop, or describes the stop without counting the degrees of freedom
1 mark: Makes a basic statement about the arm's movement, such as that it can rotate, without applying the concept
markerNotes: Degrees of freedom count independent movements, so the answer should count each rotating joint once and should not count the arm's length or reach.
The shoulder stop is a physical motion constraint, which limits the range of one joint without removing its degree of freedom.
Strong answers connect the count to the control program, which must respect the constraint when it calculates positions.
commonStudentErrors: Counting the base, shoulder and elbow as only two degrees of freedom.
Treating the stop as removing a degree of freedom, rather than limiting its range.
Stating that the arm can reach a point without linking that to the number of independent movements.
Describing the arm's appearance rather than its independent movements.

sampleAnswers.answer: The robotic arm has three degrees of freedom, because it has three independent movements: rotation of the base about a vertical axis, and rotation of the shoulder and elbow within the same vertical plane. Each of these counts as one degree of freedom, so the count excludes the arm's length and reach. The shoulder stop is a motion constraint: it limits the shoulder's rotation to 90 degrees, so the shoulder keeps its degree of freedom but can only move through part of its range. The control program must respect this limit when it calculates joint positions, so the mechatronic system never commands a movement the stop would block.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Applies the concept to count three independent movements and explains how the shoulder stop limits movement without removing a degree of freedom, which meets the full-mark standard. Naming the stop as a physical constraint on the shoulder joint would make the point sharper.

sampleAnswers.answer: The arm has three degrees of freedom: base, shoulder and elbow.
sampleAnswers.feedback: States the correct number of degrees of freedom without explaining how the shoulder stop limits movement, which earns two marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: The arm can rotate in several directions.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Makes a basic statement about movement without counting degrees of freedom or applying the concept, which earns one mark.

prompts.question: Predict how the arm's range of movement and its control program would change if the shoulder stop were removed and the elbow were locked in place, giving reasons for each prediction.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A school robotics team has a three-joint arm in which the base rotates, the shoulder and elbow rotate in one vertical plane, and a mechanical stop limits the shoulder to 90 degrees. The control program calculates joint angles to move the arm's tip to target points on a table.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Predicts both the wider range of shoulder movement and the reduced degrees of freedom, and explains how the control program and subsystem would need to change, with sound reasoning based on the motion constraints
4 marks: Predicts the effect of removing the stop and locking the elbow, with reasons that identify the change in degrees of freedom, but says little about the control program
3 marks: Predicts one effect of the changes on the arm's movement, with a brief reason
2 marks: Makes a limited prediction about the arm's movement without a clear reason
1 mark: Makes a basic statement about the arm without predicting any change
markerNotes: Strong predictions state the direction of change for each variable, such as a wider range or fewer degrees of freedom, and then give the reason.
Consider what the removed stop protected against, as well as what it limited, when predicting the arm's movement.
A locked joint changes the program's task: it no longer solves for that joint angle.
commonStudentErrors: Predicting that the arm will simply reach further, without considering the blocking of the table or the base.
Stating that locking the elbow leaves the degrees of freedom unchanged.
Describing the control program in general terms, without identifying the change it needs.
Making predictions with no reasons attached.

sampleAnswers.answer: Removing the shoulder stop, a motion constraint, would let the shoulder rotate beyond 90 degrees, widening the arm's range of movement, although parts of that range may be blocked by the base or the table. Locking the elbow would reduce the degrees of freedom from three to two, because the forearm could no longer move independently. The arm would then reach only the points on a fixed arc for each base angle, rather than any point at a chosen height and distance. The control program would need rewriting, since it would no longer calculate an elbow angle and must solve for two joint angles instead. The mechatronic system must also check each planned movement, because the stop no longer protects against over-rotation into the base or table. The arm would remain a viable subsystem for simple tasks, but it would be less flexible than before.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Predicts both the wider shoulder range and the reduced degrees of freedom, and explains how the control program and subsystem must change, with reasons, which meets the full-mark standard. Discussing which target positions would still be reachable would strengthen the prediction.

sampleAnswers.answer: Removing the stop would let the shoulder move further, so the arm could reach more of the table. Locking the elbow would make the arm less flexible.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Predicts one effect of each change with a brief reason, which earns three marks. It does not explain how the control program would change.

sampleAnswers.answer: The arm would be different.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Makes a general statement without a predicted change, which earns one mark. Predict specifically how the range changes and why.

dotPoints.description: Determine power, battery and material requirements for components of a mechatronic system

prompts.question: Calculate the power drawn by the drive motor in watts, the total current the robot draws, and the minimum battery capacity in ampere-hours for a 2-hour run, including a 20 per cent safety margin.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A small inspection robot has a 12 V drive motor that draws 3 A whenever the robot is moving. Its 12 V sensor and controller circuit draws 0.5 A at all times. The robot moves for the whole of a 2-hour run on one battery charge.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Calculates the motor power, the total current, the base battery capacity and the capacity with the 20 per cent safety margin, showing each step with correct units
3 marks: Calculates three of the four values correctly, with the safety margin omitted or incorrect
2 marks: Calculates two of the four values correctly, such as the total current and the base capacity
1 mark: Calculates one of the required values correctly, such as the motor power in watts
markerNotes: Show the formula (power equals voltage times current) and the unit for each value, since correct units are part of a full calculation.
Total the current drawn by every component that runs during the run, not only the largest load.
Applying a safety margin after the base capacity shows an understanding of design requirements for a mechatronic system.
commonStudentErrors: Using the motor current alone and ignoring the 0.5 A sensor and controller load.
Confusing ampere-hours with amps, which measure current rather than stored charge.
Adding 20 to the capacity instead of applying 20 per cent of it.
Giving power in amps or omitting the unit.

sampleAnswers.answer: The power drawn by the drive motor is P = V × I = 12 V × 3 A = 36 W. The robot's total current is 3 A + 0.5 A = 3.5 A, because the sensor and controller circuit also draws current throughout the run. Over a 2-hour run, the battery must supply 3.5 A × 2 h = 7 ampere-hours (Ah). Adding a 20 per cent safety margin gives 7 Ah × 1.2 = 8.4 Ah, so the battery for this mechatronic system should have a capacity of at least 8.4 Ah.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Calculates the power, total current, base capacity and capacity with the safety margin, each with correct units, which meets the full-mark standard. Stating the total current before the capacity makes the working easier to follow.

sampleAnswers.answer: The total current is 3 A + 0.5 A = 3.5 A. Over two hours this is 3.5 A × 2 h = 7 Ah.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Calculates the total current and the base capacity correctly, which earns two marks. It omits the motor power and the 20 per cent safety margin.

sampleAnswers.answer: The motor power is 12 V × 3 A = 36 W.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Calculates the motor power correctly, which earns one mark. Work out the total current and the battery capacity to complete the calculation.

prompts.question: Recommend a battery type and a chassis material for the inspection robot in the scenario, giving reasons that weigh weight, durability, cost and the operating conditions, to meet the material requirements of the mechatronic system.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A council is buying an inspection robot to crawl through stormwater pipes. The robot must be light enough to carry by hand, withstand wet and corrosive conditions, and run for about two hours on one charge. The design team is choosing between a lithium-ion battery and a lead-acid battery, and between an aluminium chassis and a steel chassis.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Recommends a battery and a chassis material, each justified against weight, durability, cost and the operating conditions, with accurate and well-linked reasoning
4 marks: Recommends a battery and a material with accurate reasons that address weight and operating conditions, but the trade-offs are less fully developed
3 marks: Recommends one suitable component with a relevant reason, or describes both options with some reasoning
2 marks: Describes a battery or material property with limited link to the requirements of the robot
1 mark: Makes a basic statement about a battery or material without giving a reason
markerNotes: Recommendations should weigh more than one factor, such as weight, durability, cost and the wet and corrosive conditions, and should state the trade-off.
Lithium-ion and lead-acid batteries differ in energy density, weight and sensitivity to deep discharge, and these are the points to use.
The corrosion resistance of aluminium depends on its surface treatment, so credit answers that mention anodising or coating.
commonStudentErrors: Recommending a material or battery without giving a reason.
Claiming a steel chassis is lighter than an aluminium chassis.
Ignoring the wet and corrosive conditions described in the scenario.
Discussing the advantages of one option only, without considering its cost or limitations.

sampleAnswers.answer: A lithium-ion battery is the better choice for this mechatronic system. It stores more energy for its weight than a lead-acid battery, so it can meet the required capacity in a package light enough to carry by hand. It also suffers less damage from deep discharge, although it needs a battery management circuit and suitable charging equipment. An aluminium chassis is recommended to meet the material requirements of this robot. Aluminium is lighter than steel, which reduces total weight, and it resists corrosion better when anodised or coated, which matters in wet stormwater pipes. Steel is stronger and cheaper, but it is heavier and rusts quickly in wet conditions unless protected. The main trade-off is that aluminium costs more than steel, but the council gains a lighter and more durable robot.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Recommends a battery and a material, each justified against weight, durability, cost and the wet conditions with a stated trade-off, which meets the full-mark standard. Quantifying the energy density difference would add precision.

sampleAnswers.answer: Lithium-ion batteries are lighter than lead-acid batteries, which is useful when the robot must be carried. Aluminium is light too, so it is a sensible chassis material.
