sampleAnswers.answer: The emergency stop is large and red, so a student can find it quickly. The RESTART button stops the belt starting by accident. The status display shows whether the belt is running.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes three features with general reasons they are safe, which meets the three-mark standard. Link each feature to the risk for Year 7 students to reach the higher marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: The interface should be simple so students can use it.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Makes a basic statement that the interface should be easy to use, without justifying a design choice. Name a feature and the risk it reduces.

dotPoints.description: Create and use unit tests to determine the effectiveness and repeatability of each component’s control algorithm

prompts.question: Demonstrate, using a set of test cases, how unit tests can check that the speed_for_distance function of a robot's control algorithm works as required.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student has written a function called speed_for_distance that is one component of a robot's control algorithm. It returns a motor speed of 0% when the distance is 10 cm or less, 50% when the distance is above 10 cm and up to 30 cm, and 100% when the distance is above 30 cm.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Demonstrates unit tests with a set of cases that includes boundary values and expected outputs, and explains how repeated results show effectiveness and repeatability
3 marks: Demonstrates a set of valid test cases with expected outputs, with one boundary value or the link to repeatability missing
2 marks: Demonstrates one or two test cases with expected outputs, without boundary values or a link to effectiveness or repeatability
1 mark: Identifies a unit test as a way to check a function, without a test case
markerNotes: Boundary values, such as 10 cm and 30 cm, are more informative than typical values because faults often occur at thresholds.
Each test should state an input and an expected output, so that the result can be judged as pass or fail.
Repeatability is shown by running the same test again and getting the same result, not by a single run.
commonStudentErrors: Testing only typical values, such as 20 cm, and missing faults at the thresholds.
Writing a test with no expected output, so the result cannot be judged.
Confusing repeatability, which asks whether results are consistent, with effectiveness, which asks whether the output meets the requirement.

sampleAnswers.answer:
A unit test checks one component of the control algorithm in isolation, by calling speed_for_distance with a known input. The boundary cases below test where faults are most likely:
Test case 1: input 5 cm, expected output 0%
Test case 2: input 10 cm, expected output 0%
Test case 3: input 10.5 cm, expected output 50%
Test case 4: input 30 cm, expected output 50%
Test case 5: input 31 cm, expected output 100%
Repeating the five tests with the same inputs should give the same results, which shows repeatability. Cases 2 to 5 check the thresholds, so a fault such as using < instead of <= would be caught, which shows the effectiveness of the test set.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Sets out test cases with boundary values and expected outputs, and explains how repeated results show repeatability and the effectiveness of the tests. This meets the full-mark standard.

sampleAnswers.answer: Test case 1: input 5 cm, expected output 0%. Test case 2: input 20 cm, expected output 50%.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Shows two test cases with expected outputs, but neither tests a boundary and there is no link to effectiveness or repeatability. Add a test at 10 cm and at 30 cm.

sampleAnswers.answer: A unit test checks a single function to see whether it works.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies a unit test as a way to check a function, without giving a test case. Add an input and an expected output.

prompts.question: Evaluate the effectiveness and repeatability of the speed_for_distance control algorithm, using the test results in the scenario.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: The student ran five unit tests on speed_for_distance, using inputs of 5 cm, 10 cm, 10.5 cm, 30 cm and 31 cm, and repeated each test ten times. Tests 1, 2, 3 and 5 passed in all ten runs. Test 4 used a real ultrasonic sensor held about 30 cm from a target, so its input varied between 29.8 cm and 31.2 cm, and it returned 50% in seven runs and 100% in three runs.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Evaluates the effectiveness and repeatability with sustained judgement, using the results to show the function's correctness at each input and how the test design affects repeatability, and recommends a specific fix
5 marks: Evaluates both effectiveness and repeatability using the results, identifies the cause of the variation and makes a justified judgement
4 marks: Evaluates effectiveness or repeatability using the results with a relevant reason, with limited judgement about the other
3 marks: Describes the results of one or more tests without judging effectiveness or repeatability
2 marks: Identifies whether a test passed or failed, without referring to effectiveness or repeatability
1 mark: Makes a basic statement that the tests were useful, without referring to the results
markerNotes: Separate the function's correctness from the test design, since variation in a live sensor input does not show that the function is wrong.
Use the number of runs in the scenario to support the judgement about repeatability.
A recommendation, such as a fixed input, should address the cause of the poor repeatability.
commonStudentErrors: Declaring the function unreliable because test 4 varied, without checking the inputs.
Treating a single passing run as proof of repeatability.
Describing the test results without judging whether the function is effective.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The function is effective for the four fixed-value tests. Tests 1, 2, 3 and 5 passed in all ten runs, so the speed_for_distance control algorithm returns the required speed for 5 cm, 10 cm, 10.5 cm and 31 cm. This shows the effectiveness of the function at these inputs.

The repeatability of test 4 is poor, but the cause is the test design rather than the function. The test used a real ultrasonic sensor, so the input varied between 29.8 cm and 31.2 cm. The function responded correctly to each input it received, because 29.8 cm gives 50% and 31.2 cm gives 100%, so the varying results came from the varying inputs. The unit test is therefore not repeatable because the input is not controlled.

To make the evaluation reliable, the team should replace the sensor with a fixed input of 30 cm in test 4, then repeat the test ten times. Only then can the test show whether the component is effective at exactly 30 cm. Overall, the control algorithm has shown its effectiveness, but its results cannot yet be trusted at the 30 cm boundary.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Uses the results to judge effectiveness at each fixed input, then identifies the uncontrolled sensor input as the cause of poor repeatability and recommends a specific fix. This meets the full-mark standard.

sampleAnswers.answer: Tests 1, 2, 3 and 5 passed in all ten runs. Test 4 returned 50% in seven runs and 100% in three runs.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes the results of the tests without judging effectiveness or repeatability, which meets the three-mark standard. Explain what the results show about the function and about the test design.

sampleAnswers.answer: The tests were useful for checking the speed function.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Makes a basic statement about the tests without referring to the results. Use the pass and fail data to judge the function.

dotPoints.description: Explore fundamental software development steps used by programmers when designing software (requirements definition; determining specifications; design; development; integration; testing and debugging; installation; maintenance)

prompts.question: Outline the purpose of the requirements definition step and the testing and debugging step in the software development process.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A small software team is building an online booking system for a community sports club. The project manager wants every team member to understand why requirements definition and testing and debugging are planned before any coding begins.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Outlines the purpose of both requirements definition and testing and debugging accurately, with a brief explanation of how each supports the booking system
2 marks: Outlines the purpose of both steps with limited explanation, or gives a correct purpose for only one step
1 mark: Identifies one relevant step of the software development process without stating its purpose
markerNotes: Full marks require the purpose of both steps, not just their names.
Requirements definition should be linked to what the booking system must do, such as recording members' needs before design begins.
Accept testing and debugging described as checking features against the specifications and finding and fixing defects.
commonStudentErrors: Listing the steps in order without stating what each one achieves.
Describing testing as the final step only, with no mention of finding or fixing faults.
Confusing requirements definition with designing the user interface or writing code.

sampleAnswers.answer: In the software development steps, requirements definition establishes what the booking system must do by recording what stakeholders, such as club members and administrators, need. This gives the team a clear project scope before design begins. Testing and debugging checks that each feature works as specified, and finds and fixes defects before the system is released to the club.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Gives the purpose of both steps with a specific effect for each, which meets the full-mark standard. Keep each purpose tied to the booking system to show clear understanding.

sampleAnswers.answer: Requirements definition records what the booking system must do. Testing and debugging checks that the features work and fixes faults.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Gives a correct purpose for both steps, but each explanation is brief and does not show what the step achieves for the booking system. Add one specific effect for each step to reach 3 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Requirements definition is the first step, and testing comes near the end.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies steps and their position in the process without stating a purpose for either. State what requirements definition decides and what testing and debugging achieves to earn more marks.

prompts.question: Discuss the likely consequences for a software project of skipping the requirements definition step and moving straight to design and development.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A regional council has asked a software company to build a website where residents can report potholes and broken street lights. The lead developer proposes starting coding immediately, arguing that the team can clarify what the council needs while the work progresses.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Discusses several well-developed consequences of skipping requirements definition and determining specifications, weighing how each affects cost, timeline and the final product, with a sustained link to the council scenario
5 marks: Discusses two or three clear consequences of skipping requirements definition, explaining how each affects the project, with a relevant link to the council's needs
4 marks: Discusses at least two consequences of skipping requirements definition, with an explanation of one of them in some depth
3 marks: Describes one or two relevant consequences of skipping requirements definition, with limited explanation of their effect
2 marks: Identifies a consequence of skipping requirements definition with a brief explanation
1 mark: Makes a basic statement that skipping requirements definition causes problems without explaining why
markerNotes: Credit answers that trace a chain of consequences, for example unclear requirements leading to rework and late faults found during testing and debugging.
Strong answers weigh the time saved by coding early against the later cost of rework, and reach a reasoned view.
Expect discussion of how determining specifications turns requirements into measurable targets for design and testing.
commonStudentErrors: Describing what each step is rather than discussing what happens when it is skipped.
Stating that the project will fail without naming a specific consequence.
Discussing only one consequence, such as cost, and ignoring time, quality or the council's needs.

sampleAnswers.answer: Skipping requirements definition and determining specifications, two early software development steps, would create several serious consequences for the council project. Without agreed requirements, the team cannot know what the website must do, so design and development rest on guesses. Features such as a map of reported potholes may be built, only to be rejected when the council reviews them. The rework needed to fix these features is costly, because code written before the requirements are settled must be changed or discarded, which raises the budget and delays delivery. Faults are also more likely to surface late, during testing and debugging, when they are most expensive to correct. Coding immediately may appear to save time, but the eventual result is a website that takes longer to finish and may not meet the council's needs. A sound project therefore completes requirements definition and determining specifications before development begins.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Discusses several consequences, including unneeded features, costly rework and late faults, each explained and linked to the council scenario, which meets the full-mark standard. Weighing the apparent time saving against the later cost gives the discussion a reasoned judgement.

sampleAnswers.answer: Skipping requirements definition means the team may build features the council does not need, such as a map that was never requested. The rework to fix these features adds time and cost to the project.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Discusses two consequences, with rework explained more fully than unneeded features, which meets the 4-mark standard. Develop the second consequence and link it to the council's needs to reach a higher mark.

sampleAnswers.answer: Skipping requirements definition could cause rework, so the project would cost more.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies one consequence, rework and extra cost, with a brief explanation. Add a second consequence and explain how it affects the project to lift the mark.

dotPoints.description: Research and evaluate the prevalence and use of online code collaboration tools

prompts.question: Describe two features of online code collaboration tools that allow a student team to work on the same program together.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: Three Year 11 students are building a quiz program for a school competition. They live in different suburbs and want to share their code so that each person can see the changes made by the others.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Describes two distinct features of online code collaboration tools accurately, explaining how each allows the team to share and manage the same program
3 marks: Describes two relevant features, with a brief explanation of how one of them supports the team
2 marks: Identifies two relevant features of online code collaboration tools with little or no explanation
1 mark: Identifies one relevant feature of an online code collaboration tool
markerNotes: Award the top mark for two distinct features, such as a shared repository and version control, each with a stated benefit to the team.
Accept named features such as pull requests, issue tracking or code review, provided the description explains how they help teamwork.
Explanations should refer to the team, not only describe what a tool looks like.
commonStudentErrors: Naming a tool, such as GitHub, rather than describing a feature of the tool.
Describing a feature without explaining how it helps the team work together.
Giving two features that are really the same thing, such as two names for saving code.

sampleAnswers.answer: Two features of online code collaboration tools are a shared repository and version control. A shared repository stores the program's code in one central location, so every team member works from the same up-to-date files. Version control records each change as a commit, which shows who changed what and allows the team to return to an earlier version if a fault appears. Many of these tools also support code review through pull requests, so teammates can check changes before they are merged.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes two distinct features, a shared repository and version control, and explains how each helps the team work on the same program, which meets the full-mark standard. Keep the focus on the features rather than on a named tool.

sampleAnswers.answer: A shared repository keeps the code in one place, and version control records each change so the team can see it.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies two relevant features with brief links to shared work, but the explanations are minimal. Explain how each feature helps the team to earn a higher mark.

sampleAnswers.answer: Version control is one feature of an online code collaboration tool.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies one relevant feature without explaining how it helps the team. Add a second feature and explain its benefit to earn 2 marks.

prompts.question: Evaluate the use of online code collaboration tools in software development, considering their prevalence in industry and whether they suit a student team.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A school's software engineering class is choosing a shared workspace for its Year 11 projects. The teacher knows that professional developers widely use these tools, but the students are new to version control and have limited time to learn new software.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Evaluates the use of online code collaboration tools with sustained judgement, weighing their prevalence in industry against the learning demands for students, and reaches a supported recommendation for the class
5 marks: Evaluates the use of online code collaboration tools with a clear judgement, weighing benefits such as shared repositories and code review against the learning demands for students
4 marks: Discusses the benefits and drawbacks of online code collaboration tools for a student team, with a clear link to their prevalence in industry
3 marks: Describes one or two benefits or drawbacks of online code collaboration tools, with limited link to the students' situation
2 marks: Identifies a benefit or drawback of online code collaboration tools with brief explanation
1 mark: Makes a basic statement about online code collaboration tools without evaluating them
markerNotes: Judgement must be supported by evidence, such as the wide use of Git-based platforms in industry, or the time students need to learn version control.
Credit a recommendation tied to the class's situation, for example a simplified workflow with teacher guidance.
Strong answers recognise that prevalence in industry does not by itself make a tool suitable for beginners.
commonStudentErrors: Asserting that the tools are good or bad without evidence or reasoning.
Describing features of the tools rather than evaluating their use for students.
Assuming that because professionals use a tool, it is the best choice for every learner.

sampleAnswers.answer: Online code collaboration tools are widely used in industry, so their prevalence is a strong reason to consider them in software development education. Professional teams use them to share repositories, track changes through version control and review code before it is merged, which supports quality and accountability. For a student team, these benefits are significant: everyone can see the current program, and the teacher can follow each person's contribution. However, the learning curve is real, because students new to version control may struggle with commits, branches and merge conflicts, and this can take time away from programming. The tools also add a layer of setup that a Year 11 class may not need. On balance, a student team should use these tools, but with a simplified workflow, a short introduction and clear guidelines for code review, so that the benefits are gained without overwhelming beginners.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Evaluates the use of the tools with a clear judgement, weighing prevalence in industry and benefits such as code review against the learning curve for students, which meets the full-mark standard. The recommendation is tied to the class's situation, which strengthens the judgement.

sampleAnswers.answer: Online code collaboration tools are common in industry, and they help a team share code and review changes. For students, however, the tools add a learning curve, so the teacher should introduce them gradually.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Discusses a benefit and a drawback with a link to industry, but the judgement is not developed or justified. Explain why the learning curve matters for this class to reach 5 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Online code collaboration tools let teams share code, which helps students working together.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies one benefit with a brief explanation, but there is no drawback or judgement. Add a drawback and state whether the benefits outweigh it to lift the mark.

dotPoints.description: Apply computational thinking and algorithmic design by defining the key features of standard algorithms, including sequence, selection, iteration and identifying data that should be stored

prompts.question: Apply computational thinking to a school library book-borrowing process by defining its sequence, selection and iteration, and identifying the data that should be stored.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A school library lets students borrow up to three books at a time. The library's software team needs an algorithm for checking out a book that checks the borrower's record, confirms that the book is available, and repeats the availability check for each book the student wants to borrow.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Applies computational thinking to define the sequence, selection and iteration of the checkout process accurately, and identifies the specific data that must be stored, such as the borrower ID and book ID
3 marks: Defines the sequence, selection and iteration of the checkout process with reasonable accuracy, and identifies some relevant data to be stored
2 marks: Identifies two key features of the checkout process, such as a selection or an iteration, with limited definition
1 mark: Identifies one key feature of an algorithm in the checkout process
markerNotes: Full marks need all three key features defined in the context of the checkout process, not named in general terms.
Strong answers identify data such as the borrower ID, book ID, loan date and due date, and explain why each is needed.
Accept a sequence written as ordered steps, provided the order follows from the scenario.
commonStudentErrors: Naming sequence, selection and iteration without defining them in the checkout process.
Listing data as the book's title or cover without explaining why it must be stored for the loan.
Confusing iteration with selection, such as describing a yes or no decision as a repeated step.

sampleAnswers.answer: Applying computational thinking to the checkout process gives a clear algorithmic design. The sequence is: read the borrower ID, look up the borrower record, then confirm the borrower has fewer than three books on loan. Selection checks the book's status, so if the book is available the loan is recorded, otherwise the student is told it is on loan. Iteration repeats the availability check for each book the student requests until the list is complete. The data that should be stored includes the borrower ID, the book ID, the loan date and the due date.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Defines the sequence, selection and iteration in the context of the checkout process and identifies the specific data to store, which meets the full-mark standard. Applying the features to a clear order of steps shows the algorithmic design.

sampleAnswers.answer: Sequence checks the borrower's record before the loan is recorded. Selection checks whether the book is available.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies sequence and selection with some link to the checkout process, but neither is fully defined and no data is identified. Define iteration and name the data to be stored to reach 3 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Selection is used to check whether a book is available.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies one feature, selection, correctly in the process. Add a second feature and its role in the checkout process to earn 2 marks.

prompts.question: Justify why the data that should be stored must be identified during algorithmic design, rather than after the program has been coded.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A small team is designing a program to track stock levels in a school canteen. One developer suggests writing the code first and deciding what data to store later, arguing that this will save time at the design stage.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Justifies with sustained reasoning why identifying the data to be stored during algorithmic design is essential, linking data needs to the sequence, selection and iteration of the algorithm and showing the cost of changing data after coding
5 marks: Justifies the decision to identify stored data during algorithmic design, with clear reasoning about how the data affects the sequence, selection and iteration of the algorithm
4 marks: Justifies the decision with a clear reason, such as the need to plan variables and data before coding, supported by a relevant link to the canteen program
3 marks: Gives a relevant reason why data should be planned in design, with limited development of how this affects the algorithm
2 marks: Identifies a reason data should be planned before coding, with brief or partly developed explanation
1 mark: Makes a basic statement that data matters in programs without linking it to algorithmic design
markerNotes: The justification must argue for planning data in design, not only describe what data is stored.
Strong answers explain that data decisions shape the variables, loops and decisions in the algorithm, so changing them late means rewriting logic.
Credit a response that weighs the time saved by coding first against the cost of rework, and reaches a reasoned view.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the stock data the canteen program stores without justifying why it must be planned first.
Stating that planning is good without explaining its effect on the algorithm.
Arguing that coding first saves time without considering the later cost of rework.

sampleAnswers.answer: Identifying the data that should be stored during algorithmic design is justified because the data shapes every part of the program. The sequence, selection and iteration of an algorithm depend on what is stored: the program must know which stock items to update, when a level falls below a threshold, and how many times to repeat a count. If the data is not planned first, the team cannot decide the variables, the loops or the decisions. Computational thinking supports this approach, since the team breaks the problem into the data it needs and the steps that use it. Coding first may appear to save time at the design stage, but changing the data later requires rewriting the sequence, selection and iteration already written, which costs far more time and introduces errors. Planning the data during algorithmic design therefore gives a more reliable and efficient canteen program.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Justifies identifying stored data in design with sustained reasoning, linking the data to the sequence, selection and iteration and weighing the cost of rework against the time saved by coding first, which meets the full-mark standard.

sampleAnswers.answer: Data should be planned in design because the canteen program's variables and decisions depend on what is stored, such as stock counts. If the team codes first, the sequence, selection and iteration may need to be rewritten later.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Gives a clear reason with a link to the canteen program, but does not show how changing the data late affects the algorithm in depth. Develop the cost of rework to reach 5 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Planning the stored data first helps the team write the program, because the variables depend on it.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Gives a general reason why planning helps, without explaining how the data affects the program. Name the variables or decisions that depend on the data to earn more marks.

dotPoints.description: Apply divide and conquer and backtracking as algorithmic design strategies

prompts.question: Apply divide and conquer to show how a merge sort would sort the list 7, 3, 9, 1 into ascending order.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A games club records the scores of four players in an unsorted list, 7, 3, 9, 1, and wants them ordered from lowest to highest so that the lowest score can be found quickly.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Applies divide and conquer accurately to the list, tracing each split and merge in order and explaining how the sorted subproblems combine into the final sorted list
3 marks: Applies divide and conquer with most splits and merges correct, showing how the list is divided and then recombined
2 marks: Identifies that the list is split into smaller parts and merged, with limited tracing of the steps
1 mark: Identifies divide and conquer as dividing a problem into smaller parts
markerNotes: Full marks require every split and merge to be traced correctly, not only the final sorted list.
Credit recognition that each merge combines two already-sorted lists, which is the key idea of divide and conquer.
Accept a tree diagram of the splits and merges if the steps are clearly labelled.
commonStudentErrors: Giving the sorted list without showing the splits and merges.
Merging unsorted values, such as joining 7 and 9 in the order they appear.
Describing divide and conquer in general terms without applying it to the list.

sampleAnswers.answer: Divide and conquer, used as an algorithmic design strategy, splits a problem into smaller subproblems, solves each one and then combines the results. For the list 7, 3, 9, 1, the merge sort first divides it into [7, 3] and [9, 1], then into single values [7], [3], [9] and [1]. Each pair is merged into sorted order, giving [3, 7] and [1, 9]. Finally, these two sorted lists are merged by comparing their front values in turn, producing the sorted list 1, 3, 7, 9. Each merge relies on the lists already being sorted, which is why single values can be combined in order.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Traces every split and merge in order and explains that each merge combines sorted subproblems, which meets the full-mark standard. Showing each step as a list makes the trace easy to check.

sampleAnswers.answer: Merge sort splits the list into halves until each value stands alone. Then the parts are merged back together in sorted order.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes the splitting and merging in general terms, without tracing the values in the list. Show the list after each split and merge to reach 3 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Divide and conquer splits a problem into smaller parts.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies the key idea of dividing a problem but does not apply it to the list. Trace at least one split or merge with the values 7, 3, 9, 1 to earn more marks.

prompts.question: Compare divide and conquer with backtracking as algorithmic design strategies, explaining when each is most suitable.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A software team is designing two programs for a school. One program must sort a long list of student scores. The other must solve a logic puzzle by testing possible moves, returning to an earlier move whenever a move leads to a dead end.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Compares divide and conquer and backtracking in depth, explaining how each structures the problem, the similarities and differences in their approach and when each is most suitable, supported by accurate examples
5 marks: Compares both strategies with a clear explanation of how each approaches the problem, identifying at least one similarity and one difference, and gives a suitable example for each
4 marks: Compares the two strategies by describing how each works, with at least one clear difference explained
3 marks: Describes how one or both strategies work, with limited comparison between them
2 marks: Identifies one similarity or difference between the strategies with minimal explanation
1 mark: Names divide and conquer or backtracking without comparing them
markerNotes: Strong answers identify that divide and conquer splits a problem into subproblems that are all solved and then combined, while backtracking explores candidate solutions and abandons those that cannot succeed.
Credit recognition that backtracking can stop early when a partial solution breaks a rule, which avoids exploring every option.
Suitable examples include merge sort for divide and conquer and a maze or puzzle solver for backtracking.
commonStudentErrors: Describing each strategy separately without making any comparison.
Saying backtracking is the same as searching every possibility, without mentioning abandoning dead ends.
Stating that divide and conquer is always faster, without a reason linked to the problem.

sampleAnswers.answer: Divide and conquer and backtracking are both algorithmic design strategies that break a problem into smaller parts, which is why both are often written recursively. They differ in how they approach those parts. Divide and conquer splits the problem into subproblems that are independent of each other, solves each one and combines the results. Merge sort suits the school's list of student scores, because the list is split in half, each half is sorted, and the sorted halves are merged. Backtracking, by contrast, builds a partial solution one step at a time and tests each choice against the rules. When a choice leads to a dead end, the algorithm returns to the previous step and tries another option. A logic puzzle suits backtracking because its solution depends on a sequence of choices that must be tested. In short, divide and conquer suits splitting a fixed problem into parts, whereas backtracking suits searching for a valid solution among many possible choices.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Compares the two strategies in depth, identifying a similarity and the key differences, and matches each to a suitable problem, which meets the full-mark standard. The explanation of backtracking's dead ends shows why it differs from divide and conquer.

sampleAnswers.answer: Divide and conquer splits a problem into parts that are solved and then combined, as in merge sort. Unlike this, backtracking tries a choice and returns to an earlier step when it reaches a dead end.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Compares the strategies by describing how each works and gives a clear difference, but the comparison is not developed and suitability is not discussed. Add when each strategy is most suitable to reach 5 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Both strategies break a problem into smaller parts.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies one similarity with minimal explanation. Add a difference, and explain how it affects which problems each strategy suits, to earn more marks.

dotPoints.description: Develop structured algorithms using pseudocode and flowcharts, including the use of subprograms

prompts.question: Construct pseudocode for a subprogram named Larger that returns the bigger of two numbers, and a main algorithm that calls it with the values 12 and 47.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student is building a small program for a maths quiz. The program needs a reusable subprogram that compares two numbers and sends the larger one back to the main algorithm, which then displays the result.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Constructs a structured algorithm in correct pseudocode, with a subprogram that accepts two parameters, returns the larger value and is called correctly by the main algorithm
3 marks: Constructs pseudocode with a subprogram that compares the two values correctly and returns a result, with minor errors in syntax or in how it is called
2 marks: Constructs a partly correct subprogram, such as a comparison with no return value, or a main algorithm without the call
1 mark: Identifies a comparison step in the pseudocode without a subprogram
markerNotes: Full marks require a subprogram that returns a value, not one that only displays it, and a main algorithm that calls it.
Accept any clear pseudocode form, provided the selection, the return and the call are all shown.
Credit correct use of arguments, such as 12 and 47 passed into the subprogram and the returned value displayed.
commonStudentErrors: Writing a subprogram that displays the larger value but does not return it to the main algorithm.
Writing the comparison without a subprogram, so the main algorithm is not structured.
Calling the subprogram without passing the two values, or passing values that do not match the parameters.

sampleAnswers.answer:
This pseudocode describes a structured algorithm with a subprogram that has two parameters, a and b. The selection compares them, and the subprogram's return value is the larger number.
SUBPROGRAM Larger(a, b)
  IF a > b THEN
    RETURN a
  ELSE
    RETURN b
  END IF
END SUBPROGRAM
MAIN
  result = Larger(12, 47)
  DISPLAY result
END MAIN
The main algorithm passes 12 and 47 as arguments, stores the returned value in result and displays 47.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Constructs a structured algorithm in pseudocode with a subprogram that accepts two parameters, returns the larger value and is called by the main algorithm, which meets the full-mark standard. The explanation of the return and the call shows how subprograms are used.

sampleAnswers.answer:
SUBPROGRAM Larger(a, b)
  IF a > b THEN
    RETURN a
  ELSE
    RETURN b
  END IF
END SUBPROGRAM
sampleAnswers.feedback: Constructs a correct subprogram that compares and returns a value, but the main algorithm does not call it. Add the main algorithm and its call with 12 and 47 to reach 3 marks.

prompts.question: Explain how flowcharts and pseudocode can be used together to develop a structured algorithm that includes a subprogram.

The teacher asks the student to explain how the flowchart and pseudocode can be used together when developing the game's algorithm, including a subprogram for rolling the die.

5 marks: Explains how flowcharts and pseudocode are used together in developing a structured algorithm, with a clear reason why a subprogram improves the design

sampleAnswers.answer: Flowcharts and pseudocode complement each other when developing a structured algorithm. The flowchart gives a visual overview of the dice game's control flow, so the sequence, selection and iteration can be seen at a glance: roll the die, check for a six, update the running score and repeat until the game ends. The pseudocode then turns this plan into precise steps that can be translated into code. A subprogram for rolling the die fits into both tools: in the flowchart it appears as a single predefined process symbol, which keeps the main diagram readable, and in the pseudocode it is written as a separate block with its own steps. Because the subprogram can be designed, tested and reused separately, errors in the dice logic are easier to find, and the main algorithm remains a clear, structured algorithm.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains how the flowchart and pseudocode complement each other and how a subprogram is shown in both, with sustained links to the dice game, which meets the full-mark standard. The point about designing and testing the subprogram separately gives a clear reason for its value.

sampleAnswers.answer: A flowchart shows the dice game's steps and decisions, and pseudocode writes the same steps precisely. A subprogram for rolling the die can be written as its own block, so the main algorithm stays simple.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains the roles of the flowchart and pseudocode with a relevant description of the subprogram, but the link between the two tools is not developed. Explain why a subprogram improves the design to reach 5 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: A flowchart and pseudocode both show the steps of an algorithm.

dotPoints.description: Use modelling tools including structure charts, abstraction and refinement diagrams to support top-down and bottom-up design

prompts.question: Construct a structure chart for a program that reads a student's name and three test marks, calculates the average mark and displays a report, using top-down design.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A teacher wants a program that records one student's name and three test marks, works out the average and shows a short report on screen. The program must be designed top-down, starting from a main module and breaking it into sub-modules.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Constructs a clear structure chart with a main module and correctly named sub-modules for input, calculation and output, showing the top-down design through correct connections
3 marks: Constructs a structure chart with a main module and most sub-modules correctly named and connected
2 marks: Identifies two or more modules for the program, with limited or incorrect connections between them
1 mark: Identifies one module needed by the program
markerNotes: Full marks need the sub-modules to match the task, such as input, calculation and display, with each one connected to the main module.
Accept a text or indented representation of the chart, provided the hierarchy from the main module is clear.
Credit a note that top-down design starts from the main module and refines it into smaller tasks.
commonStudentErrors: Listing the program's tasks without showing them in a hierarchy under a main module.
Drawing sub-modules that are not connected to the main module.
Naming sub-modules after variables, such as marks, rather than after tasks.

sampleAnswers.answer:
This structure chart uses top-down design. Main module: Student report
- Sub-module 1: Get student details (reads the name and the three test marks)
- Sub-module 2: Calculate average (receives the three marks and returns their average)
- Sub-module 3: Display report (shows the name and the average on screen)
Data flows from the input sub-module to the calculation sub-module, then to the display sub-module. Each sub-module performs one task, so it can be written and tested on its own, and the main module calls them in order.

sampleAnswers.answer: Main module, with sub-modules for input, calculation and display.

prompts.question: Examine how abstraction and refinement diagrams support both top-down and bottom-up design, and when each approach is more suitable.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A software company is planning two projects. One is a new attendance system built from scratch with clear requirements. The other combines several existing components, such as a login module and a report tool, that other teams have already tested.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Examines how abstraction and refinement diagrams, as modelling tools, support top-down and bottom-up design, analysing the conditions that make each approach more suitable for the two projects, with sustained and precise links to the scenario
5 marks: Examines how abstraction and refinement diagrams support both approaches, with a clear explanation of when each approach suits the projects in the scenario
4 marks: Explains the role of abstraction or refinement diagrams in top-down or bottom-up design, with a relevant link to the scenario
3 marks: Describes the features of top-down or bottom-up design, with limited reference to the modelling tools
2 marks: Identifies a modelling tool or design approach with little explanation
1 mark: Names a modelling tool used in software design without explaining its role
markerNotes: Strong answers explain that abstraction hides detail to show the big picture, and refinement adds detail level by level, so both diagrams support top-down design.
Bottom-up design builds and tests small, existing components and combines them, so it suits projects that reuse tested modules such as the login module.
Credit a judgement on suitability that refers to clear requirements for top-down design and existing tested components for bottom-up design.
commonStudentErrors: Describing abstraction and refinement as the same thing.
Stating that top-down design is always better, without a reason linked to the projects.
Describing bottom-up design as starting with the main module.

sampleAnswers.answer: Abstraction and refinement diagrams are modelling tools that support both top-down and bottom-up design, but they do so in different ways. Abstraction shows only the essential parts of the system, such as the main modules and their purpose, so the design can be understood as a whole. Refinement then adds detail level by level, breaking each module into smaller tasks, which is what a structure chart shows in top-down design. For the new attendance system with clear requirements, top-down design is more suitable: the team starts with an abstract overview, refines it step by step and only then builds the parts. Bottom-up design works in reverse, building and testing small components first and combining them. It suits the second project, because the login module and report tool have already been tested, so they can be assembled and checked without rebuilding them. Choosing the approach therefore depends on whether the requirements are clear and whether reliable components already exist.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Examines how abstraction and refinement support both approaches, analysing why top-down design suits the new system and bottom-up design suits the reuse of tested components. The judgement is tied to the scenario, which meets the full-mark standard.

sampleAnswers.answer: Abstraction shows the main modules of a system, and refinement adds detail to each module. Top-down design uses both in a new project with clear requirements, while bottom-up design suits existing tested components.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains the role of abstraction and refinement and links top-down design to the new project, but the reasons bottom-up suits the second project are brief. Develop the conditions for each approach to reach 5 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: A structure chart is a modelling tool used in top-down design.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies a modelling tool and where it is used, with little explanation. Explain what the tool shows and how it supports a design approach to earn more marks.

dotPoints.description: Analyse the logic and structure of written algorithms (determining inputs and outputs; determining the purpose of the algorithm; desk checking and peer checking; determining connections of written algorithms to other subroutines or functions)

prompts.question: Demonstrate desk checking of the written algorithm using the inputs 3, 5 and 0. Record the values of total and count after each step, and state the output.
prompts.scenario:
Hypothetical: A student has written the algorithm below to add up numbers entered by a user until a 0 is entered.
total = 0
count = 0
READ number
WHILE number <> 0
  total = total + number
  count = count + 1
  READ number
END WHILE
DISPLAY total
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Traces the written algorithm accurately with the given inputs, recording total and count after each step, and states the output of 8 with a clear conclusion about the purpose of the algorithm
3 marks: Traces the algorithm with mostly correct values and states the output of 8, with limited reference to the purpose of the algorithm
2 marks: Traces one or two steps accurately, or states the output without showing the trace
1 mark: Identifies an input or output in the written algorithm
markerNotes: Full marks need the values of total and count traced after each input, not only the final output.
Credit a conclusion that connects the trace to the inputs and outputs and the purpose of the algorithm, which is to add numbers until 0 is entered.
Accept a trace table with one row for each change, provided each value is correct.
commonStudentErrors: Stating the output without tracing the values of total and count.
Including the final 0 in the count, when the WHILE loop stops as soon as 0 is read.
Describing what the algorithm should do in general terms without using the given inputs.

sampleAnswers.answer: Desk checking traces the written algorithm line by line with test data, so its logic is checked before the program is written. Starting with total = 0 and count = 0, the first input 3 is read, so total becomes 3 and count becomes 1. The second input 5 gives total 8 and count 2. The input 0 stops the WHILE loop, so the algorithm displays total as 8. The trace table records each value, and the output of 8 matches the purpose of the algorithm, which is to add the numbers entered. This confirms that the inputs and outputs of the algorithm are handled correctly for this test.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Traces total and count after each input with correct values, then states the output of 8 and links it to the purpose of the algorithm and its inputs and outputs, which meets the full-mark standard. The trace table makes each step easy to check.

sampleAnswers.answer: Tracing the first input gives total 3 and count 1, and the algorithm displays 8 at the end.

prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses the logic and structure of the algorithm in depth, explaining why desk checking and peer checking each catch different errors in its purpose, its inputs and outputs and its call to the Average function, with a sustained conclusion
5 marks: Analyses the logic and structure of the algorithm, explaining how desk checking and peer checking each help confirm its purpose, its inputs and outputs and its connection to the Average function
4 marks: Explains how desk checking or peer checking tests the logic of the algorithm, with a relevant link to the call to the function

markerNotes: Strong answers explain that desk checking traces the algorithm's logic with test data, while peer checking uses another person's view to catch assumptions the author has missed.

sampleAnswers.answer: Both desk checking and peer checking are needed because each catches different errors in a written algorithm. Desk checking traces the logic step by step with test data, so the author can confirm that the inputs and outputs are handled correctly. For the grade algorithm, this means tracing three test marks through the decisions and checking that the displayed grade matches the purpose of the algorithm. Peer checking brings a fresh perspective: a classmate may notice an assumption the author has missed, such as a grade boundary that is wrong. The connection to the Average function must also be checked. The main algorithm must pass three values, and it must use the returned mean correctly, so a mismatch between parameters and the returned value would produce a wrong grade. Desk checking covers the trace, while peer checking covers the assumptions, so only the two together confirm that the algorithm and its subroutines or functions are correct.

prompts.question: Discuss how the choice between a procedure and a function affects the structure of the main algorithm and the way each subprogram is tested.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A programmer is writing an algorithm for a library system. One subprogram must update the loan record and show a confirmation message, while another must calculate the fine owed for a late book and return the amount to the main algorithm.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Discusses how a procedure or a function changes the structure of the main algorithm, with sustained reasoning about the return value and how each subprogram can be tested separately
4 marks: Discusses the difference between procedures and functions for the main algorithm, with a clear reason for the choice in the scenario
3 marks: Describes how a procedure or a function is used in the main algorithm, with limited discussion of the effect on structure or testing

markerNotes: Credit a discussion that explains a function's return value can be used in a calculation or decision in the main algorithm, while a procedure's effect is on the display or the record.
Strong answers explain that a function can be tested by giving it inputs and checking the value it returns.
Accept a reason that a procedure can be tested by checking its effect, such as the message displayed or the record updated.
commonStudentErrors: Describing what the two subprograms do without discussing their effect on the main algorithm.
Stating that functions are better than procedures without a reason linked to the scenario.
Assuming that a procedure can return a value to the main algorithm in the same way as a function.

sampleAnswers.answer: The choice between procedures and functions changes how the main algorithm is structured. A function returns a value, such as the fine owed for a late book, and the function's return value lets the main algorithm store it, use it in a calculation and decide what to display. The main algorithm depends on that returned value, which keeps the calculation separate from the record-keeping. A procedure performs an action, such as updating the loan record and showing a confirmation message, so the main algorithm simply calls it and carries on. A function can be tested by giving it inputs and checking the value it returns, so it can be checked in isolation. A procedure is tested by checking its effect, such as whether the record was updated. Choosing correctly therefore makes the main algorithm clearer and each subprogram easier to test.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Discusses how a function's return value and a procedure's effects shape the main algorithm, and links both to testing each subprogram separately, which meets the full-mark standard. The reasoning is sustained across structure and testing.

dotPoints.description: Experiment with object-oriented programming, imperative, logic and functional programming paradigms

prompts.question: Demonstrate the imperative and functional programming paradigms by writing pseudocode that adds the integers from 1 to 5, and state one difference between the two versions.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A Year 11 class is comparing two programming paradigms by writing the same calculation in each style. The teacher asks students to show the calculation in an imperative style and in a functional style.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Demonstrates both paradigms with correct pseudocode, using a loop that updates a variable in the imperative version and a recursive function that returns values in the functional version, and clearly states a difference between them
3 marks: Demonstrates both paradigms with mostly correct pseudocode, and states a valid difference between the two approaches
2 marks: Writes a correct version in one paradigm, or gives two partly correct versions with little difference stated
1 mark: Identifies a loop or a function as a feature of one paradigm
markerNotes: Full marks need both versions to give 15 and the difference to be explained, not just named.
Strong answers explain that the imperative version changes the variable total on each step, while the functional version calculates each result from its input without changing a stored value.
Accept any functional version that calculates from inputs without changing a stored variable, such as a recursive function.
commonStudentErrors: Writing a functional version that still changes a variable on each step, so it is imperative in style.
Stating that the imperative version is better without a reason linked to the task.
Writing the loop without stating the final output of 15.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Imperative version:
total = 0
FOR i = 1 TO 5
  total = total + i
NEXT i
DISPLAY total (output 15)
Functional version:
FUNCTION Sum(n)
  IF n = 0 THEN RETURN 0
  ELSE RETURN n + Sum(n - 1)
END FUNCTION
DISPLAY Sum(5) (output 15)
Both programming paradigms, imperative programming and functional programming, give the same output of 15, but they organise the calculation differently. sampleAnswers.answer: Both programming paradigms can represent the library, but they suit different parts of it. Object-oriented programming suits the records for books and members, because each book and member can be modelled as an object that bundles its data, such as a title or membership number, with its behaviour, such as checking out or renewing a loan. Classes act as blueprints, so new objects can be created for each new book, and inheritance can reduce repeated code for different kinds of member. Logic programming, however, suits the borrowing rules better. Facts and rules state, for example, that a member may borrow a book if the member is current and the book is available, and the system infers the answer to any query rather than following a set of instructions. The trade-off is that the object model is widely taught and familiar to many developers, while the logic model makes the rules explicit and easier to change. A sound conclusion is that object-oriented programming should structure the records, and logic programming should define the borrowing rules.

prompts.question: Explain why binary is the number system used at the hardware level of a computer, and why programmers often prefer hexadecimal to decimal when viewing memory addresses or machine code.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A programming team is debugging a low-level routine that reads raw memory addresses. Some members want the addresses shown in decimal, while others prefer hexadecimal, and the lead developer asks each member to explain the choice.

markerNotes: Credit a link between binary and the on and off states of hardware, rather than a bare statement that computers use binary.
A strong answer explains that each hexadecimal digit stands for exactly four bits, which makes long patterns shorter to read.

sampleAnswers.answer: Binary is used at the hardware level because the electronic components inside a computer, such as transistors, have two stable states, on and off. Each binary digit maps directly onto one of these states, so every value, instruction and memory address is stored as a pattern of 0s and 1s. Decimal is the number system people use every day, but it does not map naturally onto switching hardware. Hexadecimal is preferred when a programmer views a memory address or machine code because each hexadecimal digit represents exactly four bits. The byte 1111 1010 can be written as FA, which is shorter and easier to check than the binary string, and far clearer than the decimal value 250, where the bit boundaries are hidden.

prompts.question: Demonstrate, step by step, how the 8-bit two’s complement representation of the integer -23 is obtained from the positive value 23.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student is writing a program that stores a temperature change of -23 degrees in an 8-bit signed integer variable. Before writing the code, the student must work out the exact bit pattern the computer will store.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Demonstrates the full process for -23 by writing 23 in 8-bit binary, inverting every bit and adding 1 to give 11101001, with each step shown

markerNotes: Credit each step, including the inversion of every bit, rather than only the final pattern.

A check, such as converting 1110 1001 back to -23, shows that the representation is correct.

sampleAnswers.answer: Step 1: write 23 as an 8-bit binary number, which gives 0001 0111. Step 2: invert every bit, giving 1110 1000. Step 3: add 1 to the inverted pattern, giving 1110 1001. The leading bit is 1, so the value is negative. As a check, 1110 1001 is 128 + 64 + 32 + 8 + 1 = 233, and 233 - 256 = -23. This confirms that 1110 1001 is the two’s complement bit pattern for the integer -23, which the computer stores.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Every step is shown and the check confirms the final bit pattern, which meets the full-mark row.

prompts.question: Compare two’s complement with sign-and-magnitude for representing integers in 8 bits, including the range each method allows and how zero is represented.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A computing teacher is preparing a lesson on storing whole numbers in an 8-bit register. Some students suggest storing the sign as a separate bit, while others argue for two’s complement, and the teacher asks the class to compare the two methods.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Compares the two methods with sustained, precise reasoning on the sign bit, the range of each method, the two zeros of sign-and-magnitude and the single zero of two’s complement, with a clear hardware advantage
5 marks: Compares the methods in detail on at least three features, such as range and zero, with a clear similarity or difference explained for each
4 marks: Compares the methods with relevant detail on two features, such as range or zero, though one comparison is incomplete or unexplained
3 marks: Describes both methods and identifies one relevant difference, such as the two zeros of sign-and-magnitude, with limited comparison
2 marks: Identifies sign-and-magnitude or two’s complement as a method for negative integers, with a brief description of one feature
1 mark: Makes a basic statement that both methods store negative numbers, without comparing them
markerNotes: Credit a comparison that names both ranges, -127 to +127 and -128 to +127, rather than a general claim that one method is better.
Strong answers explain why a single zero matters for hardware, such as one addition circuit serving all integers.
Treating the sign bit as a similarity between the two methods, not a difference, shows real understanding.
commonStudentErrors: Describing each method separately without setting their features against each other.
Stating that both methods have the same range, which is incorrect.
Claiming that sign-and-magnitude cannot store negative integers at all.

sampleAnswers.answer: Both methods represent integers in 8 bits, but they differ in how they encode the sign. Sign-and-magnitude uses the leftmost bit as a sign bit and the other seven bits as the magnitude, so its range is -127 to +127. Zero has two representations, 0000 0000 for positive zero and 1000 0000 for negative zero, which wastes one pattern and complicates comparisons. Two’s complement also uses the leftmost bit to show the sign, but negative values are formed by inverting the bits and adding 1, so its range is -128 to +127. Zero has only one representation, 0000 0000, so the same addition circuit can handle positive and negative numbers. Two’s complement is therefore simpler and more efficient for hardware, while sign-and-magnitude needs extra logic to add and subtract numbers with different signs. The main similarity is that both methods use the leftmost bit as a sign indicator.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Compares range, zero and the sign bit for both methods and gives a supported hardware conclusion.

sampleAnswers.answer: Sign-and-magnitude uses a sign bit and seven magnitude bits, which gives two versions of zero. Two’s complement also uses a sign bit, but it has only one zero, so it is more efficient.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes both methods and one relevant difference in zero, but neither range is stated, so the comparison is limited.

sampleAnswers.answer: Both methods can store negative numbers in binary.

sampleAnswers.answer: The choice of data types affects accuracy, storage and validation. A real stored as single precision floating point gives about seven significant decimal digits, but binary rounding means a value such as 0.1 cannot be stored exactly, so a grade point average can be stored this way with acceptable tolerance, while money should not be. An integer type stores whole numbers exactly and uses less space, which suits an age or a count of cents. A char holds one character, while a string holds a sequence of characters, so a student’s initial should be a char and a full name a string, each using only the storage it needs. A date and time type lets the database reject an impossible date such as 30/02/2026, which a string could not do without extra code. prompts.question: Compare sequential files with binary search trees as data structures for storing and retrieving a large set of student records.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A school administration system holds about 1,200 student records. Staff sometimes need to find one student’s record by ID, and at the end of each year they need to print every record in ID order.

sampleAnswers.answer: Both are data structures for storing records, but they suit different tasks. Sequential files store records one after another, so finding one student means reading from the start until the matching ID is found. This is efficient for batch work, such as printing every record in ID order at year end. A binary search tree stores each record in a node, with smaller IDs to the left and larger IDs to the right, so a search takes roughly log2 of n comparisons when the tree is balanced. For 1,200 records, a balanced tree finds a student far faster, but it needs memory for pointers and must be kept balanced. Sequential files suit the year-end printout, while trees suit frequent lookups by ID.

sampleAnswers.answer: Applying computational thinking, the algorithm is converted into a subprogram that uses parameter passing: FUNCTION CountPass(marks AS array of 5 integers) RETURNS integer. Inside it, a FOR loop repeats for each mark, and an IF selection adds 1 to a counter when the mark is 50 or more. The two control structures handle the repetition and the decision. The array is one of the data structures holding the five marks, and RETURN count sends the result back to the calling program.
